findings.triggeringInput: cost (n*n row-major) = {1,9, 9,1}, n=2, match=stackalloc int[2]. Optimal bottleneck assignment is diagonal with bottleneck cost 1; Run returns 0 and leaves match[0]=match[1]=-1.
findings.rootCause: The bottleneck-assignment algorithm (e.g. binary search on threshold + bipartite feasibility / Kuhn's matching) is not implemented; only array initialization and a placeholder `return 0` exist.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement the bottleneck assignment: binary search over the sorted distinct cost values, and for each threshold test whether a perfect matching exists using only edges with cost <= threshold (Hopcroft-Karp/Kuhn). Return the minimal feasible threshold and write the matching into match[].

findings.summary: Run is an unimplemented stub: it only initializes matchLeft[]/matchRight[] to -1 and computes no assignment. For any cost matrix it returns an empty matching, which is wrong whenever an assignment of positive size exists.
findings.triggeringInput: cost (n*m row-major) = {1,2, 2,1}, n=2, m=2, matchLeft=stackalloc int[2], matchRight=stackalloc int[2]. Expected optimal assignment matchLeft[0]=0, matchLeft[1]=1; actual leaves all entries -1.
findings.rootCause: The rectangular Hungarian algorithm body is missing; only the -1 initialization loops are present.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement the O(n^2 m) Hungarian (Jonker-Volgenant style) on the n x m cost matrix, padding to square or handling the rectangular case, and write the resulting assignment into matchLeft/matchRight.

findings.summary: Run is an unimplemented stub: it initializes match[]=-1 and prices[]=0 and performs no auction iterations, so it never produces an assignment regardless of the cost matrix.
findings.triggeringInput: cost (n*n row-major) = {0,5, 5,0}, n=2, match=stackalloc int[2], prices=stackalloc int[2]. Expected an optimal assignment (e.g. match[0]=1, match[1]=0); actual leaves match all -1.
findings.rootCause: The auction bidding/price-update loop is missing; only initialization remains.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement the auction algorithm: repeated bidding rounds where unassigned bidders compute best/second-best net value, raise prices by the bid increment (plus epsilon-scaling), and reassign objects until all bidders are assigned; write final assignment to match[].

findings.summary: Run is an unimplemented stub: it only sets matchResident[i]=-1 and runs no Gale-Shapley (hospital/residents) matching, so every resident is left unmatched regardless of preferences/capacities.
findings.triggeringInput: numResidents=2, numHospitals=1, hospitalCapacities={2}, residentPref={0,0} (each resident prefers hospital 0), hospitalPref={0,1}. Stable matching assigns both residents to hospital 0 (capacity 2); actual leaves matchResident[0]=matchResident[1]=-1.
findings.rootCause: The resident-proposing Gale-Shapley loop (propose, accept up to capacity, evict worst when over capacity) is not implemented; only initialization is present.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement resident-proposing deferred acceptance using hospital preference ranks and capacities: each free resident proposes down their list; a hospital provisionally accepts while under capacity and otherwise evicts its least-preferred current resident; iterate until stable, writing matchResident[].

findings.summary: The scratch buffer is partitioned with womanRank at offset n (size n*n) but the proposal stack at offset 3n. For n>=3 these regions overlap (n + n*n > 3n), so initializing/pushing the stack corrupts womanRank entries (and vice versa), producing a wrong matching and out-of-range writes.
findings.triggeringInput: n=3 (e.g. manPref={1,0,2, 0,1,2, 0,1,2}, womanPref={0,1,2, 0,1,2, 0,1,2}); womanRank occupies scratch indices [3,12) while stack starts at scratch+9, so womanRank[w=2] (indices 9,10,11) is overwritten by the initial stack push, corrupting the rank comparison in ProcessProposal.
findings.rootCause: manNext = scratch (n ints), womanRank = scratch + n (n*n ints, occupying [n, n+n^2)), but stack = scratch + n*3. Since n + n^2 > 3n for all n > 2, the womanRank block and the stack block alias the same memory. The stack base should be scratch + n + n*n, not scratch + 3*n.
findings.suggestedFix: Place the stack after womanRank: int* stack = scratch + n + n*n; and document the required scratch size as at least n + n*n + (max stack depth, up to n*n). Apply the same correction to GaleShapley.RunWithHistory which uses the identical (buggy) layout.

findings.summary: Same scratch-partition aliasing as StableMarriage.Run: womanRank at scratch+n (size n*n) overlaps the stack placed at scratch+n*3 for n>=3, corrupting womanRank/stack data and yielding a wrong matching plus out-of-range writes.
findings.triggeringInput: n=3 with any complete preference lists (e.g. manPref/womanPref all equal to {0,1,2} per row); womanRank for w=2 lands at scratch indices 9,10,11 which the stack initialization (stack=scratch+9) overwrites before the matching loop reads them.
findings.rootCause: womanRank = scratch + n occupies [n, n+n^2) but stack = scratch + n*3; n + n^2 > 3n for n>2 so the two buffers alias.
findings.suggestedFix: Set int* stack = scratch + n + n*n; (after the womanRank block) and size scratch accordingly.

findings.summary: Run is a non-functional stub: it accepts men/women preference lists and list lengths but only initializes matchMen and matchWomen to -1 and returns, never running the Gale-Shapley with incomplete lists algorithm. Every proposer/receiver is left unmatched, so the result is wrong for any input where a non-empty stable matching exists.
findings.triggeringInput: n=1, m=1, numPrefMen[0]=1, numPrefWomen[0]=1, prefMen={0}, prefWomen={0} (man 0 and woman 0 each list the other). Expected stable matching: matchMen[0]=0, matchWomen[0]=0. Actual: matchMen[0]=-1, matchWomen[0]=-1 (both unmatched, unstable).
findings.rootCause: The method body contains no proposal/rejection loop, no preference-rank computation, and no free-proposer queue; it only performs the -1 initialization that should precede the actual algorithm. The core algorithm is entirely missing.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement the Gale-Shapley algorithm for incomplete preference lists: build rank tables for receivers, maintain a queue/stack of free proposers, have each free proposer propose down its list (length numPrefMen[i]), and let each receiver keep its most-preferred current suitor among those on its list, breaking previous tentative matches. Only leave entries at -1 when an agent genuinely cannot be matched within its list.

findings.summary: Run is a non-functional stub that unconditionally returns false and sets every match[i] to -1. The inline comment documents the return contract ('False if no stable matching exists'), so returning false when a stable matching DOES exist is a wrong result. It never runs Irving's stable roommates algorithm.
findings.triggeringInput: n=4 with the classic solvable instance, e.g. preferences pref[i] giving ranked partners: 0:[1,2,3], 1:[2,0,3], 2:[0,1,3], 3:[0,1,2]. A stable matching exists (e.g. {0-1, 2-3}), but Run returns false and leaves match all -1.
findings.rootCause: The body has no Phase 1 proposal sequence and no Phase 2 rotation-elimination logic of Irving's algorithm; it short-circuits to 'return false' after the -1 initialization, so it can never report or produce an existing stable matching.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement Irving's algorithm: Phase 1 (each participant proposes down its list, receivers hold the best proposer and reject worse, fail early if anyone exhausts its list) followed by Phase 2 (repeatedly find and eliminate all-or-nothing rotations). Return true with a filled match array when a stable matching is found, and false only after the algorithm proves none exists.

findings.summary: On a functional graph (one outgoing 'next' per node), Run is named CycleDp but sums every node visited along the walk from 'start' until the first already-visited node, including the rho-shaped TAIL that leads into the cycle. The returned maxSum therefore includes non-cycle (tail) node values, over-counting when the graph is not a pure union of disjoint cycles.
findings.triggeringInput: n=2, next=[1,1] (node 0 -> 1, node 1 -> 1 self-loop), values=[100,1]. start=0 walks nodes 0 then 1, then cur=1 is visited so it stops with sum=101. The only actual cycle is the self-loop at node 1 with sum 1, so the correct max cycle sum is 1, but Run returns 101.
findings.rootCause: The while-loop accumulates values for the entire traversal path (tail + cycle) rather than isolating the strongly-connected/cycle portion. Once it leaves any unvisited node it adds its value, so a tail node feeding into a cycle (or into a previously-visited component) is counted as part of the 'cycle' sum.
findings.suggestedFix: If the intent is the maximum cycle sum, detect the cycle entry point: record positions in the current walk, and when a node already in the CURRENT walk is hit, sum only the values from that entry point around the cycle (exclude the preceding tail). Nodes that terminate on a node visited in a PRIOR walk contribute no new cycle and should add 0. Alternatively, document that Run computes a longest walk sum on a functional graph, not a cycle sum.

findings.summary: Adjacency-list traversal uses `e != 0` as the loop terminator, but the module's graph representation uses -1 as the empty/end-of-list sentinel and 0-based edge indices (as built by TarjanScc's own test). This both (a) skips the edge stored at index 0 and (b) reads out of bounds when the chain reaches the -1 sentinel, since `-1 != 0` is true and the loop body then dereferences to[-1]/next[-1].
findings.triggeringInput: The graph from TarjanSccTests.TarjanScc_Basic: N=4, edges added in order (0->1)=e0,(1->2)=e1,(2->0)=e2,(2->3)=e3, with head[i] initialized to -1. Then head[0]==0 and the leaf vertex 3 has head[3]==-1. Calling TarjanScc.Find(4, head, next, to, tin, low, stack, inStack, sccId, ref sccCount).
findings.rootCause: In `for (int e = head[u]; e != 0; e = next[e])`, the sentinel value compared against is 0 instead of -1. Callers (and the in-module test) initialize head/next empty slots to -1 and assign edge indices starting at 0, so: edge index 0 (here head[0]=0, the 0->1 edge) is treated as 'no edge' and never visited, breaking SCC computation (vertex 0 becomes a spurious singleton SCC). Worse, when a vertex's list ends at -1 (e.g. vertex 3 with head[3]=-1), `-1 != 0` is true, so the loop enters its body and dereferences to[e]/next[e] at index -1 — an out-of-bounds pointer read (undefined behavior / crash).
findings.suggestedFix: Change the loop condition to use the -1 sentinel: `for (int e = head[u]; e != -1; e = next[e])`, matching the convention in SccAugmentation.Dfs1/Dfs2 and OnlineScc which correctly use `e != -1`.

findings.summary: BFS over the undirected adjacency list has no visited/parent guard, so every node re-enqueues its parent (and every neighbor) endlessly, overflowing the stackalloc q[n] buffer and corrupting the stack (undefined behavior / crash) for any tree with an edge.
findings.triggeringInput: n=2, root=0, an undirected edge 0<->1 represented in head/to/next (edge stored in both directions), removed all false. q starts [0]; popping 0 pushes 1; popping 1 pushes 0 again; this never terminates and writes far past q[2].
findings.rootCause: The traversal at line 51 enqueues to[e] guarded only by !removed[to[e]]; there is no visited array nor parent comparison, so in an undirected tree (each edge stored twice) the parent of u is re-enqueued, and subsequently u again, producing unbounded writes into the size-n stackalloc queue. Additionally size[u] is set to 1 but subtree sizes are never accumulated, so even without the overflow the centroid test size[to[e]] > total/2 (always 1 > total/2) is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Track the BFS parent (e.g. int* par = stackalloc int[n]; par[root]=root) and skip to[e]==par[u]; only enqueue unvisited neighbors. Then compute subtree sizes bottom-up over the BFS order before testing the centroid condition (max child subtree <= total/2 and total-size[u] <= total/2). Also replace the centroids |= (1<<u) bitmask, which cannot represent nodes u>=31, with an output array or list.

findings.summary: DP transition treats a reachable state whose accumulated weight is 0 as unreachable and skips it, dropping valid states and producing a too-small answer.
findings.triggeringInput: pathLength=2; bagSizes={1,1}; the two bags share the same single vertex; weights[that vertex]=0 (or any independent set whose best achievable weight at a mask is exactly 0). curDp[mask]==0 for a legitimately reachable mask, so line 37 `if (curDp[mask] == 0 && mask != 0) continue;` skips it and the corresponding next-layer state is never produced.
findings.rootCause: Line 37 uses the sentinel value 0 to mean 'state not reachable'. But 0 is also a perfectly valid DP value (empty selection, or vertices of weight 0). There is no separate reachability flag / -INF sentinel, so any reachable mask (other than mask 0) that currently evaluates to weight 0 is incorrectly pruned, so its forward transitions (mask-mapping at lines 41-57 and vertex introduction at lines 61-100) are never applied.
findings.suggestedFix: Initialize the dp arrays to a NEG_INF sentinel (e.g. long.MinValue/2) instead of 0, set curDp[0]=0 as the only reachable start, and change the prune to `if (curDp[mask] == NEG_INF) continue;`. Use Math.Max against NEG_INF for all relaxations and exclude NEG_INF when computing the final answer.

findings.summary: FORGET node DP slice is Max-accumulated into without being initialized, so entries of cur[] that no source mask maps to retain garbage from the caller-provided dp buffer and can corrupt the parent node's result.
findings.triggeringInput: Any nice-tree-decomposition input where a FORGET node u has a bag of size newSz=oldSz-1, the caller passes a dp buffer that is not fully zeroed (the API never documents or performs a clear), and some mask value in 0..2^newSz-1 is never produced as a target nextM. That cur[nextM] keeps the buffer's prior contents and is then consumed by ProcessIntroduce/ProcessForget/ProcessJoin of u's parent.
findings.rootCause: Line 58 does `cur[nextM] = Math.Max(cur[nextM], left[m]);` but, unlike LEAF/INTRODUCE/JOIN which fully overwrite every cur[m] they output, FORGET only relaxes targets reachable from a source mask. The remaining cur[] entries are never written, and nothing in MaxIndependentSet or ProcessForget zero-initializes the node's dp slice, so Max reads uninitialized/stale data.
findings.suggestedFix: Before the relaxation loop, clear cur[0..(1<<newSz)-1] to 0 (or a NEG_INF sentinel if unreachable states must be distinguished), e.g. `for (int m = 0; m < (1 << bSz[u]); m++) cur[m] = 0;` prior to the `for (int m = 0; m < (1 << oldSz); m++)` loop.

findings.summary: The knapsack solver is an unimplemented placeholder: it allocates and zero-clears a DP table but every node-type branch (LEAF/INTRODUCE/FORGET/JOIN) has an empty body, and the method unconditionally returns the literal 0 instead of the computed maximum value. For any non-trivial input it produces a wrong result.
findings.triggeringInput: niceNodesCount=1, nodeType={TYPE_LEAF}, leftChild/rightChild={-1,-1}, introForgetVertex={0}, bagSizes={1}, bagElements={0}, maxBagSize=1, capacity=10, weights={5}, values={100}. Expected best value 100; returns 0.
findings.rootCause: The DP transitions for the four nice-tree-decomposition node types are stubbed out (empty if/else bodies) and the function returns the constant 0 rather than reading the final answer from dp. The algorithm named TreeDecompositionKnapsack does no knapsack computation at all.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement the DP: for each nice-tree node in reverse topological order, fill dp[u][mask][c] per type (LEAF base case dp=0; INTRODUCE adds the introduced item's weight/value subject to capacity; FORGET maxes over inclusion of the forgotten vertex; JOIN combines children over c1+c2=c). Then return the maximum dp value at the root over all masks and c<=capacity instead of 0.

findings.summary: DP table size computation evaluates (capacity + 1) as 32-bit int arithmetic; for capacity == int.MaxValue this overflows to int.MinValue, making the negative factor propagate into dpSize and yield a negative/garbage allocation size cast to nint, causing a wrong/failed AllocHGlobal.
findings.triggeringInput: niceNodesCount=1, maxBagSize=0, capacity=2147483647 (int.MaxValue). (capacity + 1) overflows to -2147483648, so dpSize becomes negative.
findings.rootCause: capacity + 1 is computed in int before being promoted to long in the product, so the +1 overflows when capacity is near int.MaxValue.
findings.suggestedFix: Promote to long before adding: use ((long)capacity + 1) in the dpSize expression so the +1 cannot overflow 32-bit range.

findings.summary: In the single-centroid branch, AutomorphismCount calls AutomorphismCountRooted on a freshly stackalloc'd subHash buffer that is never populated. AutomorphismCountRooted only READS subHash[v] (line 109) to detect isomorphic sibling subtrees but never writes it, so the symmetry-factor grouping operates on uninitialized garbage, yielding a wrong automorphism count.
findings.triggeringInput: A star tree with n=4: center node 0 connected to leaves 1,2,3 (single centroid = node 0, centroidCount==1). True automorphism count is 3!=6, but with uninitialized subHash the three leaf hashes (subHash[1],subHash[2],subHash[3]) are garbage and generally unequal, so MultiplyBySymmetryFactor does not multiply by 3! and returns 1 (or some wrong value) instead of 6 mod p.
findings.rootCause: AutomorphismCountRooted depends on subHash[] already being filled by a prior CanonicalHashRooted traversal (which writes subHash[u]). The two-centroid branches first call CanonicalHashRooted (lines 83-84) to populate subHash, but the single-centroid branch at line 81 skips that step and reads uninitialized stackalloc memory. Result is non-deterministic / wrong; it is also an uninitialized-stackalloc read (UB-ish reliance on garbage).
findings.suggestedFix: In the centroidCount==1 branch, first populate subHash by calling CanonicalHashRooted(centroids[0], -1, head, to, next, subHash); before calling AutomorphismCountRooted(centroids[0], -1, ...). (Equivalently, have AutomorphismCountRooted compute and store the canonical subtree hash itself instead of assuming subHash is pre-filled.)

findings.summary: The node-merge step is a no-op, so vertices are never contracted; the global min-cut value is computed wrong for essentially any graph with n>=3.
findings.triggeringInput: n=3 triangle with unit weights: edges (0,1),(1,2),(2,0) each weight 1. Correct min cut = 2; this returns a wrong value because phases never contract s,t and the maximum-adjacency ordering never restarts on a contracted graph.
findings.rootCause: MergeNodes calls UpdateWeightsAfterPhase with add==null, and UpdateWeightsAfterPhase guards its only effect with `add != null`, so NO edge weights are ever merged from t into s. Furthermore merged nodes are marked vis[t]=-2, but FindMaxDistNode selects nodes with `vis[i] < phase`; since -2 < phase for all later phases, already-merged nodes are re-selected, so the contraction never takes effect. The Stoer-Wagner contraction is entirely missing.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement real contraction: after each phase merge t into s by, for every edge incident to t, adding weight[e] to the corresponding s-incident edge (building/maintaining an adjacency-weight matrix), permanently remove t, and reset the per-phase `vis`/`dist` state so each phase runs maximum-adjacency ordering over only the still-active (non-merged) vertices. Use a dedicated 'removed' marker distinct from the per-phase visited marker.

findings.summary: The DFS-order array `vertex` is allocated with length n but indexed up to `time == n`, writing one element past the buffer (stack buffer overflow / UB) whenever all n vertices are reachable from root.
findings.triggeringInput: n=2, root=0, single edge 0->1 (head/to/next encoding that edge). Dfs sets time=1 then recurses and sets time=2, executing `vertex[2] = 1` on `int* vertex = stackalloc int[2]`, i.e. an out-of-bounds write.
findings.rootCause: `int* vertex = stackalloc int[n];` but `time` is 1-based and reaches n when all vertices are visited, so `vertex[time]` writes index n into a size-n buffer. The reverse-order loops then also read `vertex[time]` with time up to n.
findings.suggestedFix: Allocate `vertex` with length n+1 (since time is 1-based and ranges 1..n).

findings.summary: The Lengauer-Tarjan implicit-dominator computation is wrong: idom is never seeded from the bucket processing, and the second pass uses idom[w] (always -1) plus Link with the wrong array, so idom values are not produced.
findings.triggeringInput: Any graph with n>=3 where a vertex's semidominator differs from its immediate dominator, e.g. root=0 with edges 0->1, 0->2, 1->3, 2->3 (n=4): idom[3] should be 0 but the algorithm leaves idom unresolved/-1.
findings.rootCause: Standard Lengauer-Tarjan, after `Link(parentNode[w], w)`, must immediately drain bucket[parentNode[w]] computing idom for each bucketed vertex via Eval. Here AddToBucket stores only a single vertex (bucket[v]=w overwrites), the bucket is never processed during the reverse pass, and the forward pass at lines 567-576 reads idom[w] (still -1) and calls Link(idom[u], w, ancestor, label) passing `label` as the `semi` parameter slot. As a result idom[] is left at its -1 init for most vertices.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a proper bucket list (per-vertex linked buckets, not a single int), process buckets right after each Link in the reverse pass setting idom[v] = (semi[Eval(v)]==semi[v]) ? semi[v] : Eval(v) sentinel, then finalize idom in forward order: if idom[w] != semi[w] then idom[w] = idom[idom[w]].

findings.summary: After contracting cycles and recursing, the code never expands the contracted cycles back to select the correct in-edges, so `result[]` (the parent/edge assignment) is left incorrect for vertices inside contracted cycles.
findings.triggeringInput: n=3, root=0 with edges forming a 2-cycle between 1 and 2 plus entry edges: (0->1 w=5),(1->2 w=1),(2->1 w=1). A cycle {1,2} is contracted; subRes is computed but the block at lines 151-161 contains a `while`/`for` loop with `break` that performs no assignment, so result[] for cycle vertices keeps the pre-contraction in-edge, giving a wrong arborescence.
findings.rootCause: The expansion loop at lines 151-161 is dead code: it computes nothing and immediately `break`s on the first outer iteration. The edge that enters each contracted super-node from the recursion is never mapped back to break the cycle correctly, so result[] is wrong for any input that actually requires contracting a cycle.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement cycle expansion: track for each super-node which original edge the recursion selected as its incoming edge, then for the real target vertex of that edge override result[target] and keep the cycle's other in-edges, breaking the cycle at the chosen vertex.

findings.summary: Cost transformation `maxVal - maxCost[i*n+j]` and final `(long)n * maxVal - result` can overflow Int64 for valid large long inputs, and `maxVal - minCost` overflows when costs straddle a huge range.
findings.triggeringInput: n=2 with cost matrix containing maxVal = long.MaxValue and another entry = long.MinValue: `maxVal - cost = long.MaxValue - long.MinValue` overflows long, producing a negative weight and a wrong assignment.
findings.rootCause: The min-to-max reduction subtracts each cost from maxVal without any range guard; differences can exceed long.MaxValue. Also `(long)n * maxVal` overflows when maxVal is near long.MaxValue.
findings.suggestedFix: Document a bounded input range, or perform the negation/transform in a wider domain (e.g. Int128) or by negating costs (cost -> -cost) and running the min solver directly instead of the maxVal-subtraction trick.

findings.summary: The explicit DFS stack is sized stackalloc int[n], but vertices are pushed every time they are seen as an unvisited neighbor (before being marked visited at pop time), so a vertex can be pushed many times and the stack index exceeds n, causing an out-of-bounds write (stack buffer overflow / UB).
findings.triggeringInput: Complete graph K4: n=4, undirected edges {0-1,0-2,0-3,1-2,1-3,2-3} stored as a forward-star (each undirected edge as two directed arcs). Start=0 pushes 1,2,3; popping 3 (still all of 1,2 unvisited) pushes 1 and 2 again, making top reach 4 and writing stack[4] out of the stackalloc int[4] buffer.
findings.rootCause: Marking visited[u]=true happens only when u is popped, not when it is pushed; combined with the for-loop pushing every currently-unvisited neighbor, a single vertex is enqueued multiple times, so the number of live stack entries can be O(m) >> n while the buffer is only n.
findings.suggestedFix: Mark a vertex visited at push time (set visited[v]=true and parent[v]=u immediately before stack[++top]=v) and skip pushing already-visited vertices, OR size the stack to hold the worst case. Marking-on-push also fixes the parallel/duplicate-push correctness issue. Keep the stack within [0,n).

findings.summary: The 0-1 BFS deque dq is a circular buffer of fixed size n, but vertices are (re)inserted on every distance improvement with no visited/finalized guard, so the number of simultaneously queued elements (cnt) can exceed n; the circular indices then wrap and overwrite still-pending entries, corrupting the queue and producing wrong distances.
findings.triggeringInput: n=3, start=0, edges (forward-star): 0->1 w=0, 0->2 w=0, 1->2 w=0, 2->1 w=0 (a small graph where multiple zero-weight relaxations re-enqueue 1 and 2). Repeated front-insertions/back-insertions drive cnt above n=3, wrapping dh/dt over live slots.
findings.rootCause: Standard 0-1 BFS may push a vertex more than once; a circular array sized exactly n cannot hold more than n live entries. With only dist-improvement checks (no 'is finalized' check) the deque can hold more than n pending items, so dh/dt wraparound overwrites unprocessed vertices.
findings.suggestedFix: Either guard relaxation with a finalized[] flag and skip stale pops (each vertex finalized once), or size the deque to a safe upper bound (e.g. 2*m+1) instead of n so wraparound cannot overwrite live entries.

findings.summary: Visited state is tracked via parent[v]==-1, but the start vertex keeps parent[start]==-1 for the whole run, so any edge pointing back to start treats start as unvisited and re-pushes it, causing re-traversal (and potential stack overflow on cycles through start).
findings.triggeringInput: n=2, start=0, adjacency containing edge 0->1 and 1->0. Processing node 1's edge to 0 finds parent[0]==-1, so it sets parent[0]=1 and pushes 0 again, re-running the DFS subtree and overwriting depth[0].
findings.rootCause: parent[start] is left at the sentinel -1 that doubles as the 'unvisited' marker; the start vertex is therefore indistinguishable from an unvisited vertex, so back-edges into start re-enqueue it.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a dedicated visited[] array (or set parent[start]=start as a self-sentinel and test for that) so the start vertex is recognized as visited and never re-pushed.

findings.summary: cutU/cutV are allocated with stackalloc int[m] inside the body of the iterations loop (run Math.Max(5,n*n) times). C# does not release stackalloc memory per loop iteration; it accumulates until the method returns, so the stack grows by 2*m ints per iteration and overflows for moderate n and m.
findings.triggeringInput: n=200, m=2000: iterations = n*n = 40000, each allocating cutU+cutV = 2*2000 ints = 16000 bytes, accumulating to ~640 MB of stack space, far beyond the thread stack limit -> stack overflow.
findings.rootCause: stackalloc inside a loop allocates fresh stack space each iteration without freeing previous iterations' allocations; placing the per-iteration scratch buffers (cutU, cutV) inside the loop makes total stack usage proportional to iterations*m.
findings.suggestedFix: Hoist the cutU/cutV stackalloc above the iterations loop (allocate once, reuse each iteration), or allocate them via the heap/Marshal so loop-iteration stack growth is bounded.

findings.summary: Johnson's per-source Dijkstra uses the wrong reduced edge weight: it adds h[s] (the source potential) instead of h[u] (the edge-tail potential). The reduced cost of edge u->v must be w + h[u] - h[v], but line 360 computes 'd + ew[i] + h[s] - h[v]'. This makes the algorithm's reweighting incorrect on any path with an intermediate vertex u != s, so shortest distances are wrong precisely on the negative-edge graphs Johnson exists to handle.
findings.triggeringInput: n=3, m=2, edges (0->1, w=-1) and (1->2, w=-1). Potentials become h[0]=0, h[1]=-1, h[2]=-2. Run returns dist[0*3+2] = -1, but the true shortest distance 0->2 is -2.
findings.rootCause: Line 360 'long nd = d + ew[i] + h[s] - h[v];' references the source potential h[s] rather than the current vertex's potential h[u]. The reduced weight w(u,v)+h[u]-h[v] is what keeps the un-reduction at line 373 (dist - h[s] + h[t]) consistent; using h[s] in the relaxation breaks that invariant by an additive error of (h[s]-h[u]) per traversed edge.
findings.suggestedFix: Change line 360 to 'long nd = d + ew[i] + h[u] - h[v];' (use the edge tail u, not the source s).

findings.summary: Johnson.Run returns bool (signalling feasibility, like BellmanFord.Run which returns false on a negative cycle) but never detects negative cycles. After the n Bellman-Ford relaxation passes over the augmented graph it unconditionally returns true, so on a graph containing a negative cycle it claims success and writes meaningless (non-converged) potentials and distances.
findings.triggeringInput: n=2, m=2, edges (0->1, w=-1) and (1->0, w=-1): a negative cycle. Run returns true and dist[] contains garbage instead of returning false.
findings.rootCause: No post-relaxation check: after the Bellman-Ford loop (lines 329-342) there is no extra pass verifying that no edge can still be relaxed, and the method ends with an unconditional 'return true;' at line 376.
findings.suggestedFix: After computing bfDist, run one more pass over all m+n augmented edges; if any edge with bfDist[uu] != long.MaxValue can still relax bfDist[vv], return false to signal a negative cycle.

findings.summary: ProcessEulerianCircuit (used by the public EulerianOrientation) allocates a fixed Hierholzer stack of 1024 ints ('stackalloc int[1024]', commented 'Simplified stack size'), but the stack depth grows with the number of edges traversed (up to ~m+1). For any graph with m >= 1024 edges in a single circuit, 'stack[ss++] = v' writes past the 1024-element buffer, corrupting the stack frame / adjacent stackalloc memory (undefined behavior).
findings.triggeringInput: A connected even-degree graph with m = 2000 edges (e.g. a single cycle of 2000 edges) passed to EulerianOrientation; the Hierholzer traversal pushes well over 1024 vertices, overflowing stack[1024].
findings.rootCause: Line 134 'int* stack = stackalloc int[1024];' hardcodes a capacity unrelated to n or m, while the algorithm can push up to m+1 entries before any pop.
findings.suggestedFix: Size the stack from the actual edge count, e.g. 'int* stack = stackalloc int[m + 1];' (or accept a caller-provided scratch buffer), so capacity matches the maximum Hierholzer stack depth.

findings.summary: The 0-1 BFS deque is a circular buffer of exactly n ints, but the algorithm performs no in-queue deduplication: a vertex is (re)enqueued on every strict distance improvement, so the same vertex can occupy several live slots and the number of simultaneously queued entries (cnt) can exceed n. When cnt > n the head/tail wrap (dh<0 -> n-1, dt>=n -> 0) overwrite still-live entries, corrupting the queue and producing wrong distances / reading stale vertex ids.
findings.triggeringInput: n=5, start=0, edges: 0->1(w1), 0->3(w1), 0->4(w1), 0->2(w0), 2->1(w0), 2->3(w0). After popping 0 the deque holds {2 (front), 1,3,4} (cnt=4); popping 2 front-pushes both 1 and 3 (their dist drops 1->0), driving cnt to 6 > n=5 and overwriting a live slot in the size-5 buffer.
findings.rootCause: The deque 'dq' is allocated as stackalloc int[n] (line 386) and there is no inqueue/dedup guard, yet a dedup-free 0-1 BFS deque can hold more than n entries; the wrap-around arithmetic assumes total live entries never exceed n.
findings.suggestedFix: Allocate the deque with capacity for the worst case (e.g. 2*n, or m+1) since a vertex may be pushed multiple times, or add an in-queue check to bound simultaneous entries to n.

findings.summary: Out-of-bounds read/write on C and B: the update loop indexes up to C[n]/B[n] but both arrays are length n (valid indices 0..n-1), so the last iteration writes/reads one element past the buffer.
findings.triggeringInput: s = {1,1,1,1} (long[4]), n = 4, c = long[5]. At i=0, d = s[0] = 1 != 0 and 2*L(=0) <= 0, so Run calls UpdateBM(C,B,n=4,m=0,d=1,b=1,replaceB=true). The loop 'for(j=0; j<=n-m; j++)' becomes j=0..4, and at j=4 it executes 'C[0+4] -= coef*B[4]' = C[4]/B[4], both indices == n == 4, out of the length-4 stackalloc.
findings.rootCause: C and B are stackalloc long[n], but Berlekamp-Massey needs polynomial coefficient arrays of size n+1 (a degree-L feedback polynomial has L+1 coefficients and L can reach n). The loop bound 'j <= n - m' with m as small as 0 makes m+j reach n, and B[j] reaches B[n]. The read-modify-write 'C[m+j] -= coef*B[j]' touches C[n]/B[n] regardless of B[j] being zero, which is OOB (UB) on the stack. The same defect appears in Run's final copy 'for(i=0;i<=L;i++) c[i]=C[i]' and the discrepancy loop reading C/s, where L can equal n.
findings.suggestedFix: Allocate C and B as stackalloc long[n + 1] (and require caller c to be size n+1), or equivalently tighten the loop so m+j never reaches n. Initialize the extra slot to 0. This restores the standard BM invariant that the feedback polynomial may have degree up to n.

findings.summary: For an order-1 recurrence (k == 1) the line 'res[1] = 1' writes index 1 of a length-1 stackalloc, an out-of-bounds stack write (UB).
findings.triggeringInput: k = 1, init = {5} (long[1]), trans = {3} (long[1]) representing a[i] = 3*a[i-1] with a[0]=5, n = 2, mod = 1000000007. Since n(2) >= k(1), execution reaches 'res = stackalloc long[1]' (length 1) and then 'res[1] = 1', which writes one element past the buffer.
findings.rootCause: The code initializes the polynomial state with pol[0]=1 and res[1]=1, implicitly assuming k >= 2 so that res has at least two slots. Order-1 linear recurrences (e.g. geometric sequences) are valid inputs with k = 1, but res only has k = 1 element, so res[1] is OOB. The subsequent x^? loop and reduction then operate on corrupted/OOB state.
findings.suggestedFix: Handle k == 1 specially (x mod (x - trans[0]) reduces to the scalar trans[0], so the answer is trans[0]^(n-k+1) applied to init), or size the working polynomials to max(k, 2) and clamp the initial 'res[1] = 1' so it is only written when k >= 2, performing the first reduction step explicitly for k == 1.

findings.summary: Modular exponentiation does plain long multiplication (res*a%mod and a*a%mod) without overflow-safe multiplication. For any modulus larger than floor(sqrt(long.MaxValue)) = 3037000499, the intermediate product a*a (with a up to mod-1) overflows signed 64-bit, wrapping to a negative/garbage value and producing a wrong result.
findings.triggeringInput: Run(a=3999999999, e=2, mod=4000000000): a%=mod -> 3999999999; a*a = 15999999992000000001 overflows long.MaxValue (9223372036854775807), wrapping negative; the returned value does not equal (3999999999^2) mod 4000000000.
findings.rootCause: Line 11 computes 'res = res * a % mod' and 'a = a * a % mod' directly in long arithmetic. With mod > sqrt(long.MaxValue) ~ 3.037e9, operands < mod can have products exceeding long range, so the multiply overflows before the % mod is applied.
findings.suggestedFix: Route the multiplications through SafeMulMod.Run (after that routine itself is fixed) instead of raw '* % mod', e.g. res = SafeMulMod.Run(res, a, mod); a = SafeMulMod.Run(a, a, mod); or use Int128/UInt128 for the product.

findings.summary: The large-modulus path (mod > int.MaxValue) reduces a*b via repeated doubling/addition using SafeAdd, which computes 'a + b' in plain long arithmetic. When the modulus exceeds long.MaxValue/2 (~4.61e18), operands a,b in [0,mod) can sum to more than long.MaxValue, overflowing to a negative value and corrupting the result. The routine is named 'Safe' but is not safe for the upper half of the valid long modulus range.
findings.triggeringInput: Run(a=mod-1, b=mod-1, mod=(1L<<62)+5 = 4611686018427387909): inside the doubling loop SafeAdd(a,a,mod) computes (4611686018427387908 + 4611686018427387908) = 9223372036854775816 > long.MaxValue (9223372036854775807), overflowing to a negative number; result is wrong.
findings.rootCause: Line 96 'long res = a + b; return res >= mod ? res - mod : res;' assumes a+b does not overflow long. That holds only when mod <= long.MaxValue/2. For mod in (long.MaxValue/2, long.MaxValue], a+b can overflow signed 64-bit before the comparison, so the conditional subtraction operates on a wrapped negative value.
findings.suggestedFix: Detect overflow before subtracting: 'ulong s = (ulong)a + (ulong)b; if (s >= (ulong)mod) s -= (ulong)mod; return (long)s;' (unsigned sum cannot overflow since a,b < mod <= long.MaxValue, and a+b < 2*long.MaxValue < ulong.MaxValue), or use Int128.

findings.summary: BigIntPow uses fixed-size stackalloc int[1000] buffers for cur/temp/ans, but the result of a^e can have far more than 1000 decimal digits, causing out-of-bounds writes (stack corruption / UB) and a wrong/truncated result for representable inputs the method contract does not exclude.
findings.triggeringInput: a = single digit 2 (n=1, a[0]=2), e=4000. Then 2^4000 has 1205 decimal digits. BigIntMul writes results past the end of the 1000-element stackalloc 'ans'/'cur'/'temp' buffers.
findings.rootCause: The buffers cur, temp, ans are hard-coded to 1000 ints. There is no precondition bounding e or the digit-length of the result, so any base/exponent whose power exceeds 1000 digits overflows these stack buffers. BigIntMul.Run(ansLen, ans, curLen, cur, temp) and the subsequent copy loops (for i<ansLen: ans[i]=temp[i]) index up to the true product length (n+m of the operands), which can exceed 1000, writing out of bounds and corrupting the stack.
findings.suggestedFix: Size the buffers to the maximum possible result length, which is bounded by n * e digits (i.e. allocate based on n*e, e.g. stackalloc int[n*e + 1] or a caller-supplied scratch length), or document and enforce a precondition on the maximum result size. Replace the magic 1000 with a length derived from n and e.

findings.summary: When low==0, the value 1 is never marked non-prime and is incorrectly reported as prime. Line 45 only marks index 0 (value 0) false for low==0; value 1 lives at index 1 and is handled only in the separate low==1 branch (line 46), so for a block starting at 0 the integer 1 escapes both the special-case marks and the sieving loop (the smallest prime p marks from start=p*2, never touching value 1).
findings.triggeringInput: low=0, high=5, with a valid base primes array {2,3} (primeCount=2). result will include 1 as a prime: output contains 1.
findings.rootCause: The special handling distinguishes low==0 vs low==1 but for low==0 it marks only index 0 (the integer 0) and forgets that the integer 1 (at index 1) must also be marked composite. The main sieving loop starts each prime at p*2, so 1 is never crossed off.
findings.suggestedFix: When low==0 (i.e. the block covers the integer 1), also set isPrime[1-low]=isPrime[1]=false. E.g. after marking index 0: `if (low <= 1 && high >= 1) isPrime[1 - low] = false;` and remove the bogus Math.Min(0L,size-1) construct.

findings.summary: Absolute-value negation overflows for MinValue inputs: `if (a < 0) a = -a;` leaves a == MinValue (negation of MinValue wraps to itself), so the Euclidean loop runs on a still-negative operand and returns a negative/wrong gcd. The code explicitly normalizes sign of negative inputs, so negative arguments (including MinValue) are within its claimed contract.
findings.triggeringInput: Gcd.Run(-6, int.MinValue) returns -2 instead of 2 (true gcd of -6 and -2^31). Likewise Gcd.Run(-6L, long.MinValue) returns a negative value instead of 2.
findings.rootCause: -int.MinValue (and -long.MinValue) is not representable in two's complement and wraps back to MinValue, so the sign-normalization `a = -a` silently fails, leaving a negative operand in the loop and producing a negative gcd.
findings.suggestedFix: Negate the OTHER operand for the MinValue case or compute gcd on unsigned magnitudes. E.g. cast to ulong/uint magnitudes (ulong ua = a < 0 ? (ulong)(-(a+1)) + 1UL : (ulong)a;) run the loop in unsigned space, and return the magnitude; or document that MinValue is excluded. The result must always be non-negative.

findings.summary: Lcm does not normalize the sign of its inputs and returns a negative value for negative operands. It calls Gcd (which returns a non-negative gcd for normal inputs) but computes `a / g * b` using the original signed a and b, so a single negative argument yields a negative 'lcm'.
findings.triggeringInput: Lcm.Run(-4, 6) returns -12 instead of 12. (Both int and long overloads.)
findings.rootCause: `a / g * b` preserves the sign of a*b; with one negative argument the product is negative. LCM is defined as non-negative, so the result is wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Take absolute values of a and b before computing, e.g. compute on |a| and |b| (guarding against MinValue), so the returned lcm is always non-negative. If only positive inputs are intended, document that contract.

findings.summary: Modular inverse fails (returns -1 "no inverse") for negative inputs whose true gcd with mod is 1, because ExtendedGcd returns a NEGATIVE gcd g for negative a, so the check `g != 1` is wrong.
findings.triggeringInput: ModInv.Run(a=-1, mod=2): ExtendedGcd returns g = -1 (not +1), so `g != 1` is true and the method returns -1, but the inverse of -1 ≡ 1 (mod 2) is 1. Also ModInv.Run(-3, ...) family: any negative a where the Euclidean reduction reaches a negative base value (e.g. a=-1 mod=2, a=-3 mod=50, a=-41 mod=50) yields g = -1.
findings.rootCause: ExtendedGcd.Run(a, mod, ...) returns the raw value `a` at its base case, which is signed and can be negative when the initial `a` is negative (C# `%` is sign-preserving). The mathematical gcd is |g|, so for a valid coprime negative input the true gcd is 1 while g = -1. ModInv only accepts `g == 1`, so it incorrectly reports no inverse for genuinely invertible negative residues. ModDiv.Run inherits this: ModDiv.Run(1, -1, 2) returns the -1 error sentinel instead of 1.
findings.suggestedFix: Compare the magnitude: use `if (g != 1 && g != -1) return -1;` (or normalize the gcd sign), then `return ModNormalize.Run(x, mod);` (ModNormalize already maps any x into [0,mod), so the negative-g sign on x is handled there). Equivalently, reduce a with ModNormalize before calling ExtendedGcd so the first argument is always non-negative.

findings.summary: Modular addition overflows long for valid residue inputs when mod > long.MaxValue/2, producing a garbage (often negative) result instead of (a+b) mod mod.
findings.triggeringInput: ModAdd.Run(a=4999999999999999999, b=4999999999999999999, mod=5000000000000000000). Both a,b are valid residues in [0,mod). `a+b` overflows Int64 to a negative value, `r >= mod` is false, and the method returns -8446744073709551618 instead of the correct 4999999999999999998 (mod-2).
findings.rootCause: `long r = a + b;` is computed without overflow protection. For inputs in [0,mod), a+b can reach 2*mod-2; when mod exceeds long.MaxValue/2 (~4.61e18) this exceeds Int64.MaxValue and wraps. The sibling ModMul deliberately uses an overflow-safe doubling scheme, indicating the library intends to support near-long moduli, so this addition path is inconsistent and wrong for the same input domain.
findings.suggestedFix: Use an overflow-safe form, e.g. `if (a >= mod - b) r = a - (mod - b); else r = a + b;` (assuming a,b already in [0,mod)), or compute via the same compare-before-add trick used in ModMul.Run line 22.

findings.summary: Bit packing produces corrupted output because the 32-bit `buffer` cannot hold the carry, and the post-flush shift `(int)((uint)buffer >> 32)` is a no-op (C# masks the shift count by &31, so >>32 == >>0), so the flushed bits are never cleared and high bits of straddling values are silently lost.
findings.triggeringInput: bits=1, len=33, src = all 1s. Expected packed words dst[0]=0xFFFFFFFF, dst[1]=0x00000001. Actual: after i=31 the flush leaves buffer unchanged (0xFFFFFFFF) and bitCount=0, then i=32 ORs into the still-full buffer, yielding dst[1]=0xFFFFFFFF. Also bits=20,len=2,src={1,0xFFFFF}: bits 32..39 of the second value never enter the 32-bit buffer and are lost.
findings.rootCause: `buffer` is `int` (32 bits) but the algorithm assumes it can retain up to 31 residual bits plus a new value before flushing; `src[i] << bitCount` discards bits beyond bit 31, and `buffer = (int)((uint)buffer >> 32)` evaluates to `buffer >> 0` (shift count masked to 0 per ECMA-335 / C# spec) instead of 0, so the word is never cleared after being emitted.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a 64-bit accumulator: `ulong buffer; buffer |= (ulong)(uint)src[i] << bitCount; while (bitCount >= 32) { dst[outIdx++] = (int)(uint)buffer; buffer >>= 32; bitCount -= 32; }`. The final `buffer >>= 32` on a `ulong` shifts by a valid 0..63 count and correctly clears the emitted word.

findings.summary: Bit unpacking corrupts values that straddle a 32-bit word boundary: residual bits sit in the low part of the 32-bit `buffer`, then `buffer |= src[i] << bitCount` shifts the new 32-bit word left by `bitCount` and loses its top `bitCount` bits, so values spanning two source words are reconstructed incorrectly.
findings.triggeringInput: bits=20, len=2, srcLen=2, with a value packed across the word boundary (e.g. compressing {1, 0xFFFFF} then decompressing). The second decoded value comes back missing its top bits instead of 0xFFFFF.
findings.rootCause: `buffer` is a 32-bit `int`; after extracting a value `bitCount` residual bits remain in `buffer`, and `buffer |= src[i] << bitCount` with `bitCount` up to `bits-1` shifts the freshly read 32-bit word past bit 31, discarding its high `bitCount` bits. A 32-bit accumulator cannot simultaneously hold leftover bits and a full incoming 32-bit word.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a 64-bit accumulator: `ulong buffer; buffer |= (ulong)(uint)src[i] << bitCount; bitCount += 32; ... dst[outIdx++] = (int)(buffer & mask); buffer >>= bits; bitCount -= bits;` so no bits are dropped when residual and new word coexist.

findings.summary: BitCount infinite-loops on any negative input because `x >>= 1` is an arithmetic (sign-propagating) shift, so negative values never reach 0.
findings.triggeringInput: BitCount.Run(-1) (int overload) or BitCount.Run(-1L) (long overload): the loop condition `x != 0` is never satisfied because -1 >> 1 == -1, hanging forever.
findings.rootCause: Population count is computed by repeatedly testing `x & 1` and doing `x >>= 1`; for signed types `>>` is arithmetic, so negative inputs sign-extend and the high bit is never cleared, producing an infinite loop. No contract restricts the input to non-negative.
findings.suggestedFix: Use the unsigned/logical shift `>>>` (cast to uint/ulong first), e.g. iterate over `(uint)x` / `(ulong)x` with `x >>>= 1`, or use `System.Numerics.BitOperations.PopCount`.

findings.summary: BitLength infinite-loops on any negative input because `x >>= 1` arithmetic-shifts a negative value, which never becomes 0.
findings.triggeringInput: BitLength.Run(-1) or BitLength.Run(-1L): the while loop never terminates since -1 >> 1 == -1. This also makes NextBit.Run(0x80000000-pattern) and any caller passing a negative hang.
findings.rootCause: Bit length is computed by counting how many `x >>= 1` operations are needed to reach 0; the signed arithmetic shift sign-extends negatives, so the loop never ends. No contract restricts input to non-negative.
findings.suggestedFix: Use logical shift `>>>` (or cast to uint/ulong) so the sign bit is shifted out, or compute via `32 - LeadingZeroCount((uint)x)` / `64 - LeadingZeroCount((ulong)x)`.

findings.summary: In the large-n branch (n > b), Phi calls GetPhi(n, n, b, preSumLarge, ...) WITHOUT ever populating preSumLarge via SievePhi. GetPhi returns preSum[x] for every x <= b, but preSumLarge is the raw, uninitialized caller buffer, so the entire recursion reads garbage and the returned prefix sum is wrong.
findings.triggeringInput: DuJiao.Phi(100000, preSumLarge, memo, memoized) with valid buffers. b = max(10000, 100000^(2/3)) = 10000, so n > b. Returns 2078303198 vs correct sum_{i<=100000} phi(i) = 3039650754. Any n > 10000 hits this path.
findings.rootCause: SievePhi((int)b, preSumLarge) is only invoked in the n<=b short-circuit branch (line 12). The large branch (lines 14-17) skips the sieve entirely, so preSum[x] for x<=b is never computed; GetPhi (line 111: 'if (x <= b) return preSum[x];') reads uninitialized memory.
findings.suggestedFix: Before calling GetPhi in the large branch, sieve the small block: call SievePhi((int)b, preSumLarge) (sieving up to b, not n) so preSum[1..b] is filled. Likewise the buffer/sieve must cover indices up to b.

findings.summary: Same defect as Phi: in the large-n branch Mobius calls GetMobius(n, n, b, preSumLarge, ...) without first calling SieveMobius to populate preSumLarge. GetMobius's base case 'if (x <= b) return preSum[x];' then reads the uninitialized caller buffer, producing a wrong Mobius prefix sum.
findings.triggeringInput: DuJiao.Mobius(100000, preSumLarge, memo, memoized). b=10000 so n>b. Returns garbage (e.g. -11764787) vs correct sum_{i<=100000} mu(i) = -48. Any n > 10000 is wrong.
findings.rootCause: SieveMobius((int)limit, preSumLarge) is only called in the n<=b branch (line 35). The large branch (lines 37-40) never fills preSumLarge, so GetMobius (line 127) reads uninitialized memory.
findings.suggestedFix: In the large branch, call SieveMobius((int)b, preSumLarge) to fill preSum[1..b] before invoking GetMobius.

findings.summary: The Stern-Brocot mediant walk is incorrect: it produces wrong ranks for most fractions and enters an infinite loop for others. r,s are initialized to 1,0 and never updated, so the convergence check 'if (a==r && b==s) break;' (s stays 0, b stays >0) can never fire, and the per-iteration update does not correctly walk the Farey sequence.
findings.triggeringInput: FareyRank.Run(1, 3, 5) never terminates (infinite loop / hang). FareyRank.Run(2, 5, 5) returns 2 but 2/5 is the 5th element of F_5 (0/1,1/5,1/4,1/3,2/5,...). FareyRank.Run(1, 4, 5) returns 2 (expect 3). FareyRank.Run(1, 1, 5) returns 1 via the a==b early-return (expect 11).
findings.rootCause: The algorithm's recurrence and termination condition are wrong: 'r' and 's' are dead constants (never reassigned), so the loop relies only on 't <= 0' to stop, which for inputs like 1/3 and 1/2 never becomes true; meanwhile for fractions where it does stop it almost always stops after one step yielding rank 2. The 'a==0 || a==b => return 1' early-out also gives the wrong rank for a==b (1/1 is the last term, not the first).
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a correct Farey-rank algorithm: rank(a/b, n) = (number of irreducible fractions p/q <= a/b with q<=n). A standard approach computes count = sum_{q=1}^{n} floor(a*q/b) then subtracts via Mobius/inclusion-exclusion to count only reduced fractions (or use the recursive count C(a,b,n)=sum floor((a*q)/b) and Mobius-correct). Remove the broken Stern-Brocot walk and fix the a==b base case.

findings.summary: Loop guard 'i * i <= n' overflows long for n near long.MaxValue. When i exceeds sqrt(n), i*i can wrap to a negative value, which is <= n, so the loop never terminates as intended and writes divisors out of the caller's buffer (out-of-bounds / never-ending growth).
findings.triggeringInput: Divisors.Run(long.MaxValue, divs). At i=3037000500, i*i overflows to -9223372036709301616, and (-9223372036709301616 <= long.MaxValue) is true, so the loop continues past sqrt(n) writing beyond the intended divisor count (OOB writes / runaway).
findings.rootCause: i*i is computed as a long multiplication with no overflow guard; for n > (long)sqrt(long.MaxValue)^2 region the product wraps negative and the comparison i*i <= n stays true forever.
findings.suggestedFix: Use 'i <= n / i' as the loop guard instead of 'i * i <= n', or cap i with a precomputed integer sqrt(n) and compare i*i only when safe.

findings.summary: Forward zeta-over-multiples transform iterates d in DESCENDING order (d=n..1), which double-counts. For the in-place accumulation f[d]+=f[j] (j a multiple of d) to equal sum_{d|i} f[i], d must be iterated ASCENDING so f[2d], f[3d]... still hold their ORIGINAL values when read. With descending d, f[2d] has already absorbed f[4d],f[6d]... before f[d] reads it, so multiples-of-multiples are counted multiple times and f[d] is wrong for any d that has a multiple chain (already wrong at n=4).
findings.triggeringInput: f = [_, 1, 1, 1, 1] (1-indexed, n=4). Forward gives f[1]=1+f[2]+f[3]+f[4]; but f[2] was already updated to 1+f[4]=2, so f[1]=1+2+1+1=5 instead of the correct sum_{1|i}f[i]=4. Concretely a=[_,1,1,1,1],b=[_,1,1,1,1],n=4: Run yields wrong result vs the true gcd-convolution.
findings.rootCause: In-place divisor-zeta accumulation requires ascending outer index so multiples are read before they are themselves modified; descending order reads already-mutated (over-counted) multiple entries.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the outer loop to ascending: `for (int d = 1; d <= n; d++)` in Forward.

findings.summary: Inverse (Mobius inversion of the multiples-zeta) is wrong twofold: (1) it multiplies by mu[j/d], but the in-place inverse of the in-place zeta is NOT a single Mobius-weighted pass — the correct in-place inverse is simply f[d] -= sum_{j=2d,3d,..} f[j] (no mu weighting, since the divisor-zeta/Mobius cancellation telescopes when done in-place); and (2) it iterates d ASCENDING, but the in-place subtractive inverse must iterate d DESCENDING so the multiple entries f[j] still hold their (not-yet-inverted) zeta values when subtracted. Both errors make Run produce wrong gcd-convolution output.
findings.triggeringInput: a=[_,1,1,1,1], b=[_,1,1,1,1], n=4, mu computed correctly. After a correct Forward, Inverse(result,...) returns result[1] etc. not equal to the brute-force h[k]=sum_{gcd(i,j)=k}a[i]b[j]. Verified mismatch at n=4 (e.g. random a=[_,*],b=[_,*] over [-9,9] gives result[1] off, e.g. got -5 want -17 for one seed).
findings.rootCause: Misformulated inverse: applied a Mobius-weighted single pass in ascending order instead of the in-place descending subtractive inverse f[d]-=f[j]; the mu array and j/d indexing are spurious for an in-place transform.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace Inverse body with descending plain difference: `for (int d = n; d >= 1; d--) for (int j = 2*d; j <= n; j += d) f[d] -= f[j];`. The mu parameter is then unused (can be dropped, along with mu from Run).

findings.summary: Forward divisor-zeta double-counts: it reads f[d] after f[d] has already been overwritten by its own smaller divisors in the same pass, so the result is not the intended divisor-sum F[j]=sum_{d|j} f[d]. The class name 'LcmConvolution' relies on this being the exact zeta transform whose Mobius inverse is undone by Inverse, but it is a different (and not cleanly invertible by mu) linear map.
findings.triggeringInput: f[1..4] = {1,2,3,4}, n=4 -> Forward produces f[4]=8 instead of the correct divisor-sum F[4]=1+2+4=7 (f[4] erroneously adds the already-inflated f[2]=1+2=3). Likewise f[8],f[12],etc. are wrong.
findings.rootCause: The naive 'for d=1..n: for j=2d..n step d: f[j]+=f[d]' loop processes d in increasing order and reads the live (already-modified) f[d]. By the time d is used as a source, f[d] has accumulated contributions from divisors of d, so those contributions are double-added into every multiple of d. A correct divisor-sum zeta must add the ORIGINAL f[d] (e.g. iterate over primes: for each prime p, for j with j*p<=n: f[j*p]+=f[j], in increasing j), not the running value.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement the linear-time prime-based divisor zeta: requires a smallest/largest-prime factorization (or a primes list). For each prime p (ascending) and each j with p*j<=n in increasing j, do f[p*j]+=f[j] only along the prime-power chain so each divisor's original contribution is counted exactly once; or precompute and use the standard SOS-over-divisors transform that reads source values before they are mutated.

findings.summary: Inverse (Mobius) transform has the same structural flaw and does not invert even the correct divisor-sum zeta: 'f[j] -= mu[j/d]*f[d]' reads the live f[d], which has already been modified by larger divisors processed earlier in the descending loop, so the result is wrong and Run's roundtrip does not recover the input.
findings.triggeringInput: Take F = correct divisor-sum of orig=[_,1,2,..,12] (n=12); applying Inverse yields rec[2]=4 (should be 2), rec[4]=10 (should be 4), rec[6]=18 (should be 6), etc. — orig is not recovered.
findings.rootCause: Like Forward, the loop 'for d=n..1: for j=2d..n step d: f[j]-=mu[j/d]*f[d]' uses the running f[d] instead of either the transformed value F[d] or the already-restored original f[d] in a consistent order, so the Mobius inversion is applied against a mix of partially-updated values. A linear Mobius inversion must process along prime chains reading source values before mutation, mirroring a correct Forward.
findings.suggestedFix: Pair the inverse with the prime-based forward: for each prime p (descending or ascending per the chosen forward) and each j with p*j<=n in the matching order, subtract along the prime-power chain so each Mobius term reads the correct (already finalized for that step) value. Verify with a roundtrip test that Inverse(Forward(f))==f for random f.

findings.summary: Inner sieve loop computes the composite-marking start index as `i * 2` (and steps `j += i`) in 32-bit int arithmetic; for sufficiently large n the prime `i` exceeds 2^30 and `i*2` overflows to a negative int, so multiples of `i` are never marked composite, yielding wrong prime lists and wrong PrimePi/PrimeSum/MultiplicativeSum results.
findings.triggeringInput: PrimePi(n=1152921504606846976 /* 2^60 */, ...): maxV=(int)sqrt(n)=1073741824 fits int, but the first prime i>1073741823 makes `i*2` overflow int.MaxValue. Even earlier, e.g. n=1300000000000000000 produces maxV~1.14e9 and primes i in (2^30, maxV] whose `i*2` overflows.
findings.rootCause: `for (int j = i * 2; j <= maxV; j += i)` uses int*int for the start index. When i > int.MaxValue/2 (~1.07e9), `i*2` overflows to negative, the loop body is skipped (or `j += i` wraps), so composites with smallest factor i are left marked prime. maxV can legitimately reach near int.MaxValue for n approaching ~4.6e18 (all within long contract).
findings.suggestedFix: Use a wider start index, e.g. `for (long j = (long)i * 2; j <= maxV; j += i) isPrime[(int)j] = false;`, keeping j as long to avoid the int overflow.

findings.summary: MultiplicativeSum combines g0 (prime count) and g1 (prime sum) as f(p)=c0+c1*p, but UpdateMultiplicativeBlocks only sieves g0; g1 is never reduced from 'sum of all integers <= val' to 'sum of primes <= val' (the code even comments the g1 update is missing). For any c1 != 0 the prime-base values g[i] are wrong, producing an incorrect multiplicative sum.
findings.triggeringInput: MultiplicativeSum(n=10, c0=0, c1=1, fPower=(p,e)=>p^e (identity on primes), mod=1000000007, ...): expected sum over k<=10 of a multiplicative f with f(p)=p equals (e.g.) sum of all integers' value under that f; g1[*] stays as 1+2+...+val instead of (sum of primes <= val), so g[idx] and SolveS return wrong results. Concretely for n=10 the base prime sum should be 2+3+5+7=17, but g1 is left as 1+2+...+10=55 minus 1 => 54.
findings.rootCause: InitializeMultiplicativeBlocks sets g1 to the full triangular-number sum (sum of all integers in [2,val]); UpdateMultiplicativeBlocks performs the inclusion-exclusion sieve only on g0 and omits the analogous g1 = g1 - p*(g1[idx]-prefixPrimeSum) update. Thus g1 never becomes the prime-restricted sum required by line 114's `c1*g1`.
findings.suggestedFix: Add the g1 sieve step mirroring PrimeSum's UpdatePrimeSumBlocks: maintain a prefix sum sp of primes and update `g1[j] = (g1[j] - p%mod*(g1[idx]-sp[i]+mod)%mod + mod)%mod;` inside the same inner loop as the g0 update.

findings.summary: The linear-sieve inner loop computes the candidate composite as a 32-bit int ('i * primes[j]' in the loop condition on line 38, and 'i * p' on lines 41, 44, 49). For large n the product i*primes[j] exceeds int.MaxValue and wraps to a negative value. The wrapped negative value still satisfies '<= n', so the loop body executes and writes isPrime[i*p] / mu[i*p] at a negative (out-of-bounds) index, corrupting memory and producing wrong Mobius values. The sibling class MobiusSieve.cs (line 27) correctly casts with '(long)i * primes[j]', confirming the intended guard is missing here.
findings.triggeringInput: n = 2000000000 (caller supplies result/mu/isPrime arrays of size n+1, primes large enough). When the outer index reaches i = 1200000000 with primes[0] = 2, the condition 'i * primes[0] <= n' evaluates 2400000000 which overflows int32 to -1894967296; that is <= n, so the body runs 'isPrime[-1894967296] = false', a negative out-of-bounds write. Any n where some i*primes[j] crosses 2^31 while i*primes[j-1] <= n triggers it.
findings.rootCause: Product of two ints used both in the loop-bound comparison and as an array index without widening to long; 32-bit overflow yields a negative value that passes the '<= n' test and is then used to index isPrime/mu.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the product as long, exactly like MobiusSieve: use 'long product = (long)i * primes[j];' guard the loop with 'product <= n' and index with '(int)product' only after the bound check. E.g. replace the for-condition and body accesses to use the long product.

findings.summary: maxA is computed with (long)Math.Sqrt((double)(limit/b3)) and the inner loop emits a*a*b3 up to a==maxA with NO guard that a*a*b3 <= limit. Math.Sqrt overshoots for many large arguments (the double result rounds up to an m where m*m > x), so a==maxA can produce a powerful number strictly greater than limit, which is wrongly included in the output set.
findings.rootCause: Floating-point sqrt of a 64-bit integer is not exact for large values; (long)Math.Sqrt can return a value whose square exceeds the original. The generation loop trusts maxA blindly instead of bounding the product against limit, so it can emit a*a*b3 > limit.
findings.suggestedFix: After computing maxA via Math.Sqrt, correct it with a loop (while (maxA*maxA*b3 > limit) maxA--; while ((maxA+1)*(maxA+1)*b3 <= limit) maxA++;), or test 'a*a*b3 <= limit' inside the loop before emitting/continuing. This eliminates both the overshoot (emitting > limit) and the symmetric undershoot (missing a valid value).

findings.summary: The long overload factors a 64-bit n but stores each prime factor into int* via (int)p / (int)n. Trial division allows p up to floor(sqrt(n)) (~3.03e9 > int.MaxValue) and the final large-prime cofactor can be up to n (~9.2e18). Both casts to int silently overflow, recording a wrong (truncated/negative) prime value while the rest of factorization (exponents, count) proceeds, producing an incorrect factorization for valid long inputs.
findings.triggeringInput: n = 5000000029 (a prime > 2^31). Trial loop finds no factor (sqrt ~ 70710), then the n>1 branch stores outPrimes[0] = (int)5000000029 = 705032733 (wrong prime), exponent 1. Also n = 4840000004400000001 (= 2200000001^2): the factor p = 2200000001 > int.MaxValue is stored as (int)2200000001, a negative/wrong value.
findings.rootCause: Mismatch between the 64-bit input domain and 32-bit output storage: prime factors of a long can exceed int.MaxValue (both interior factors up to sqrt(n) and the residual large prime up to n), but they are written through int* with an unchecked (int) cast.
findings.suggestedFix: Make outPrimes a long* (and store p / n directly as long), or restrict the documented contract of this overload to n whose every prime factor fits in int and validate accordingly. Changing the output buffer to long* is the correct fix for a general long factorization routine.

findings.summary: Prime factors of phi(n) are stored in an int* buffer via (int)p / (int)tmp. When phi(n) has a prime factor exceeding int.MaxValue (2^31-1), the cast truncates it (often to a negative value), so phi/factors[i] yields a wrong (e.g. negative) exponent. ModPow with a non-positive exponent returns 1 because its `while (e>0)` loop never executes, making the order test `PowMod(g,exp,n)==1` always true; every candidate g is rejected and Run returns -1, failing to find a primitive root that actually exists.
findings.triggeringInput: n = 4294967387 (a prime; phi(n)=n-1=2*2147483693 where the prime factor 2147483693 > int.MaxValue). Run returns -1 even though g=2 is a valid primitive root.
findings.rootCause: `int* factors = stackalloc int[64];` plus `factors[fc++] = (int)p;` and `if (tmp > 1) factors[fc++] = (int)tmp;` narrow a long prime factor to int. For factors > 2^31-1 this overflows/becomes negative, then `phi / factors[i]` produces a wrong exponent and ModPow(g, negativeExp, n) returns 1 unconditionally (its loop guard is `while (e > 0)`).
findings.suggestedFix: Store factors as long: declare `long* factors = stackalloc long[64];` and use `factors[fc++] = p;` / `factors[fc++] = tmp;` (remove the (int) casts). This keeps full-range prime factors so `phi / factors[i]` and the subsequent PowMod test are correct for all long n.

findings.summary: Integer division by zero in the step-count formulas crashes (DivideByZeroException) on essentially every input, including the very first iteration for simple fractions.
findings.triggeringInput: Run(0, 1, num, den, depth): a=0,b=1,c=1,dd=0 -> medNum=1,medDen=1,cmp=1*1-0*1=1>0 -> denom = n*b - a*d = 0*1 - 0*1 = 0 -> division by zero on iteration 1. Also Run(2,1,...) crashes on the second iteration (denom n*b-a*d = 2*1-2*1 = 0). A brute-force over n,d in 0..10 shows division by zero for every pair.
findings.rootCause: When cmp>0 the code divides by (n*b - a*d) and when cmp<0 it divides by (c*d - n*dd). These quantities equal the cross-product distance from the current left/right boundary fraction to the target n/d, which becomes exactly 0 whenever the boundary coincides with (a rational multiple of) the target — which happens routinely, e.g. immediately when n=0 or after the first jump lands a boundary on the target. The accelerated step count uses the wrong denominator (it should divide by the distance of the OPPOSITE boundary / mediant, never one that can be zero) and there is no guard against a zero denominator.
findings.suggestedFix: Guard each division: if the denominator is 0 (or use the standard Stern-Brocot/continued-fraction stepping where the divisor is the cross product against the moving boundary that is strictly nonzero), fall back to a single mediant step. Concretely, compute steps only when the denominator != 0, otherwise take steps=1; and verify the formula divides by (c*d - n*dd) consistently in BOTH branches with sign handling, since that term is the one bounded away from zero until cmp==0.

findings.summary: Next(bound) can return a NEGATIVE value because it computes a signed long modulo of a SplitMix64 output whose high bit is often set; the contract (and all callers) require a result in [0, bound).
findings.triggeringInput: With the default seed 123456789, the SECOND call to RandomInt.Next(100) returns -90 (SplitMix64 yields seed = -9222453836012030090, and -...090 % 100 = -90 in C#). Any bound works; e.g. RandomInt.Next(100) returns negative on roughly half of all draws.
findings.rootCause: _seed % bound (line 19 and line 42) uses signed remainder. SplitMix64.Run returns (long)u where the top bit is frequently set, so _seed is negative ~50% of the time, and C# 'negative % positive' is negative. Range() (lo + Next(...)) then returns values below lo, and RandomShuffle.Run uses Next(i+1) as an index j which can be negative.
findings.suggestedFix: Reduce in unsigned space and only then take the result, e.g. return (int)((ulong)_seed % (uint)bound); for Next, and (long)((ulong)_seed % (ulong)bound); for Next64. (Note this also still has modulo bias, but the correctness defect is the negative return.)

findings.summary: Out-of-bounds pointer write because the swap index j = RandomInt.Next(i+1) can be negative, since RandomInt.Next does not guarantee a non-negative result.
findings.triggeringInput: Run(ptr, len) with any len >= 2 using the default RandomInt seed: the draw RandomInt.Next(i+1) returns a negative j (e.g. -90 for the default-seed second draw), then ptr[j] = ... writes before the buffer (memory corruption / UB). Also when j is negative the Fisher-Yates is not a valid permutation.
findings.rootCause: RandomShuffle relies on RandomInt.Next returning a uniform value in [0, i], but Next can return a negative number (see the RandomInt.Next finding). j < 0 makes ptr[j] read/write out of the allocated range.
findings.suggestedFix: Fix RandomInt.Next to return a non-negative value (unsigned modulo). No change needed here once Next is correct, but Run is the place where the negative index manifests as memory corruption.

findings.summary: int overflow in 'i * i' (loop bound and i2) for large n leads to a negative i2 and an out-of-bounds negative-index write into result.
findings.triggeringInput: Prefix(2000000000, result) (n is a valid non-negative int). At i=46341, i*i overflows int to -2147479015, so the loop condition 'i*i <= n' is true, i2 = -2147479015, and the inner loop 'for (j = i2; j <= n; j += i2) result[j] = 0;' starts with a huge negative j -> result[j] writes far out of bounds (UB), and the squarefree marking is also wrong.
findings.rootCause: Lines 44 and 46: 'for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; i++)' and 'int i2 = i * i;' use 32-bit multiplication. For n above ~2.1e9-region (any n with floor(sqrt(n)) such that i*i exceeds int.MaxValue), i*i wraps to negative.
findings.suggestedFix: Use a long for the square comparison and i2: 'for (int i = 2; (long)i * i <= n; i++) { long i2 = (long)i * i; for (long j = i2; j <= n; j += i2) result[(int)j] = 0; }' (or cap i at (int)Math.Sqrt(n)).

findings.summary: (int)Math.Sqrt(n) overflows int for large n, making 'limit' negative; the sieve and summation loops then do not run and Count returns 0 instead of the true squarefree count.
findings.triggeringInput: Count(9223372030926249001, mu) (a valid n > 0, this is 3037000499^2). Math.Sqrt(n) ~= 3.037e9 > int.MaxValue, so (int) conversion yields a negative/undefined value; limit < 0 => SieveMobius loops skip, the d-loop skips, and the method returns 0, whereas the real count is large.
findings.rootCause: Line 20: 'int limit = (int)Math.Sqrt((double)n);'. For n > ~4.6e18 the square root exceeds int.MaxValue and the cast overflows. Count's only documented precondition is n > 0 (line 16-18), so such n is in-contract.
findings.suggestedFix: Store limit as long, or check that the sqrt fits in int; e.g. 'long limit = (long)Math.Sqrt((double)n); while ((limit+1)*(limit+1) <= n) limit++; while (limit*limit > n) limit--;' and iterate d as long. (Practically Count is bounded by the caller-supplied mu size, but the cast should not silently overflow to a wrong answer.)

findings.summary: The p ≡ 3 (mod 4) fast path returns ModPow(a,(p+1)/4,p) without verifying that the result actually squares back to a. For a quadratic NON-residue it returns a bogus value instead of -1, so Run() reports a wrong square root for non-residues even though the general (p ≡ 1 mod 4) path correctly returns -1 for them.
findings.triggeringInput: Run(a=3, p=7): 3 is a non-residue mod 7 (squares mod 7 are {0,1,2,4}). Fast path computes ModPow(3,(7+1)/4=2,7)=9 mod 7=2, and Run returns min(2,5)=2, but 2^2=4≠3 mod 7. Expected return value is -1.
findings.rootCause: Unlike the general branch which detects non-residues via the inner loop (i==m -> return -1), the (p & 3)==3 branch unconditionally returns the exponentiation result. For a non-residue, a^((p+1)/4) is a square root of -a (not a), so it is not a valid sqrt of a, and no residue check is performed.
findings.suggestedFix: After computing r = ModPow(a,(p+1)>>2,p) in the p≡3(mod4) branch, verify ModMul(r,r,p)==a%p; if not, return -1. The general path's non-residue detection should be mirrored here.

findings.summary: The linear-sieve inner-loop guard `i * primes[j] <= n` and the subsequent index `isPrime[i * p]` compute `i * primes[j]` in 32-bit int. For large valid int n, this product overflows int before the comparison, wraps to a negative value that passes the `<= n` guard, and is then used as an array index, causing an out-of-bounds/negative-index pointer write (UB) and a corrupted sieve.
findings.triggeringInput: n = 2_100_000_000 (a valid int). When i = 1_100_000_000, i * primes[0] = i*2 = 2_200_000_000 overflows int32 to -2_094_967_296, which is <= n, so the loop body runs and writes isPrime[-2_094_967_296] (out-of-bounds write).
findings.rootCause: i, primes[j], p and n are all int; the multiplication i*primes[j] (and i*p) is performed in 32-bit arithmetic and can exceed int.MaxValue for n within the int contract, overflowing before the bound check and before being used as an index.
findings.suggestedFix: Perform the guard in 64-bit: `(long)i * primes[j] <= n`, and compute the index once as `long idx = (long)i * p;` using it for isPrime/phi only when idx <= n (and confirm phi multiplications also stay in range).

findings.summary: NextFloat returns a value in the CLOSED interval [0,1] (divides by 4294967295.0f, which itself rounds up to 2^32 in float, so top results yield exactly 1.0f). Then activeIdx = (int)(NextFloat(ref rng) * activeCount) can equal activeCount, indexing active[activeCount] which is one past the last valid active element. This reads a stale/zero-initialized stack slot and uses it as 'center', so candidates are generated around a wrong (garbage / origin) point instead of a real active sample — corrupting the spatial distribution.
findings.triggeringInput: Any seed/state for which NextFloat() == 1.0f at the line 'int activeIdx = (int)(NextFloat(ref rng) * activeCount);' while activeCount >= 1 (e.g. rng state whose mangled 'result' falls in the top range that rounds to 2^32; reachable for some seed). With activeCount=1 this selects active[1], an unwritten slot.
findings.rootCause: Mapping uint32 to float by dividing by 4294967295.0f (= 2^32-1). In float32 the divisor and the maximum dividend both round to 4294967296.0f, so the result reaches and can even exceed 1.0, making (int)(value*n) reach n. The index is never clamped to [0, activeCount-1].
findings.suggestedFix: Divide by 4294967296.0f (2^32) to produce a half-open [0,1) range, OR clamp the result: 'if (result_float >= 1f) result_float = 0.99999994f;', OR clamp the index: 'activeIdx = activeIdx >= activeCount ? activeCount - 1 : activeIdx;'. Same fix needed for the first-point generation and angle/radius which assume [0,1).

findings.summary: Identical defect to the 2D version: NextFloat divides by 4294967295.0f and can return exactly 1.0f, so activeIdx = (int)(NextFloat(ref rng) * activeCount) can equal activeCount and read active[activeCount], one element past the valid range, yielding a garbage center for candidate generation.
findings.triggeringInput: Any seed whose NextFloat() evaluates to 1.0f at 'int activeIdx = (int)(NextFloat(ref rng) * activeCount);' with activeCount >= 1 (top-range uint result that rounds to 2^32 in float).
findings.rootCause: uint-to-float scaling by (2^32 - 1) instead of 2^32; float rounding makes the result inclusive of 1.0, and the active-index is never clamped.
findings.suggestedFix: Divide by 4294967296.0f to get [0,1), or clamp activeIdx to activeCount-1 / clamp NextFloat below 1.0.

findings.summary: gridSize = gridW * gridH * gridD is computed as a 32-bit int product of three per-axis cell counts derived from (max-min)/cellSize. For representable, contract-valid bounds and minDistance this triple product overflows int32, producing a negative or wrapped gridSize that is then passed to 'stackalloc int[gridSize]', causing a crash / undefined behavior (and even when positive it attempts a multi-gigabyte stack allocation).
findings.triggeringInput: min=(0,0,0), max=(2000,2000,2000), minDistance=0.05, seed arbitrary, maxPoints>=1. cellSize=0.05/1.7320508=0.02887, gridW=gridH=gridD=ceil(2000/0.02887)=69283; gridW*gridH*gridD = 69283^3 overflows int32 -> negative gridSize -> stackalloc int[negative].
findings.rootCause: Per-axis grid extents are large for small minDistance / large domains, and their product is taken in 32-bit signed arithmetic with no overflow guard or size cap before stackalloc.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the product in long and guard it (e.g. if ((long)gridW*gridH*gridD > someCap) bail out / use a heap or hashed grid), and never stackalloc a runtime-unbounded size. The 2D version has the same class of issue (gridW*gridH) for large domains; both should use a checked 64-bit size and a bound.

findings.summary: The Chirp-Z / Bluestein transform builds the kernel h symmetrically as h[n-1+i] = h[n-1-i] = d^(-C(i,2)), i.e. it uses C(|k-i|,2) as the convolution exponent. But C(x,2)=x(x-1)/2 is not symmetric (C(1,2)=0 vs C(-1,2)=1), so the Bluestein identity i*k = C(i,2)+C(k,2)-C(k-i,2) requires the SIGNED value C(k-i,2). For terms where i>k the exponent of d is wrong, so res[k] is incorrect for every k except k=0. The whole transform produces wrong output for any n>=2.
findings.triggeringInput: mod=998244353, n=5, a=[random nonzero], c,d arbitrary nonzero generators. E.g. a={938753228,...}: true CZT res[1] should differ from computed; verified numerically that only res[0] matches and res[1..n-1] are all wrong.
findings.rootCause: h[n-1-i] (the lower convolution half) is set to FastPow(invD, C(i,2)) instead of the value that yields the signed exponent C(k-i,2). Because the kernel is mirrored using the magnitude of k-i rather than its sign, the convolution prod[n-1+k] = sum_i g[i]*d^(-C(|k-i|,2)) gives exponent C(i,2)-C(|k-i|,2)+C(k,2), which equals i*k only when i<=k. For i>k the exponent is off, corrupting the result.
findings.suggestedFix: The mirrored kernel must encode d^(-C(j,2)) where j = (k - i) is allowed to be negative. Reformulate so the convolution produces exponent C(i,2) + C(k,2) - C(k-i,2) with the signed (k-i). Concretely, precompute w[t] = d^(C(t,2)) for t in [-(n-1)..(n-1)] using the actual signed t (t(t-1)/2, which differs for negative t), build g[i]=a[i]*c^i*d^(-C(i,2)) and h indexed so that h[k-i] picks d^(C(k-i,2)) for the true signed difference, then res[k] = (sum) * d^(-C(k,2)). Do not collapse the two halves to the same FastPow(invD,C(i,2)) value.
