findings.rootCause: The return type was left as int while the data type was widened to long; the (int) cast truncates the high bits of any long median value outside the int range.
findings.suggestedFix: Change the return type of RunInt64 to long and remove the (int) cast: return sorted[l + (len >> 1)];

findings.summary: Even-count running median computed as (maxHeap[0]+minHeap[0])>>1 overflows signed long when the two middle values are large, producing a grossly wrong (often negative) median.
findings.triggeringInput: n=2, a=[long.MaxValue, long.MaxValue]. res[1] is computed as (long.MaxValue+long.MaxValue)>>1 which overflows to -1 instead of long.MaxValue.
findings.rootCause: Line 97 sums the two middle heap tops before halving: (maxHeap[0] + minHeap[0]) >> 1. The intermediate sum can exceed long range for representable inputs (e.g. two values near long.MaxValue, or two large negatives near long.MinValue), wrapping around. The returned/stored median for that step (and any step with an even prefix length whose two medians sum out of range) is then wrong.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the midpoint without overflow: res[i] = (maxSize+minSize)%2==0 ? maxHeap[0] + ((minHeap[0] - maxHeap[0]) >> 1) : maxHeap[0]; (note maxHeap[0] <= minHeap[0] by the heap invariant, so minHeap[0]-maxHeap[0] is non-negative and cannot overflow).

findings.summary: Scalar return value is res[(n-1)/2] (median of only the first (n-1)/2+1 elements), not the median of all n elements; disagrees with the obvious intent of returning the final overall median.
findings.triggeringInput: n=4, a=[1,2,3,4]. The per-step output res[3]=2 is the correct median of all four elements, but the method returns res[(4-1)/2]=res[1]=1 (median of just [1,2]).
findings.rootCause: Line 99 returns res[(n-1)/2]. The res[] array stores the running median after each prefix; index (n-1)/2 selects the median of a strict prefix rather than index n-1 (the full-array median). For any even-length array, or any n>1 where the prefix median differs from the overall median, the scalar return is not the median of the input.
findings.suggestedFix: If the scalar result is meant to be the overall median, return res[n-1] instead of res[(n-1)/2]. If a prefix median is genuinely intended, document it; as written the return value contradicts the method's name and the fully-correct res[] output.

findings.summary: Superset enumeration is fundamentally wrong: it only adds the single smallest free bit each step (super = super + smallest), walking one monotone chain from subMask up to maxMask instead of enumerating all 2^k supersets over the k free bits. It emits roughly k+1 masks instead of 2^k, and the masks it does emit are not the distinct supersets. For subMask=0b001, maxMask=0b111 it returns 3 masks (001,011,111) when there are 4 supersets (001,011,101,111); 0b101 is never produced. A brute-force cross-check over all (subMask,maxMask) pairs with maxMask<256 found 5281/6561 inputs produce a wrong count.
findings.triggeringInput: subMask=0b001 (1), maxMask=0b111 (7): returns count=3 and dst={1,3,7}, missing superset 0b101 (5); correct result is 4 masks {1,3,5,7}.
findings.rootCause: The algorithm treats superset generation as a single ascending walk: at each step it takes the lowest free bit (add = maxMask & ~super; smallest = add & -add) and does super = super + smallest. This deterministically fills bits from low to high along one path and reaches maxMask after k additions, so it visits only the k+1 masks on that chain and never the other 2^k - (k+1) supersets formed by other combinations of the free bits. 'super + smallest' also only behaves like a set-bit because that bit is guaranteed clear, but the enumeration logic itself is wrong. The unused 'remaining = maxMask ^ subMask' confirms the intent to range over free bits, which the code fails to do.
findings.suggestedFix: Enumerate subsets of the free-bit set and OR onto subMask. e.g.: int free = maxMask & ~subMask; int s = free; int count = 0; while (true) { dst[count++] = subMask | s; if (s == 0) break; s = (s - 1) & free; } return count; This emits exactly 2^popcount(free) distinct supersets (including subMask itself when s==0 and maxMask when s==free).

findings.summary: Generic Run<T> reinterprets the element bytes as int/long and sums them with integer arithmetic. For floating-point element types (float has sizeof==4, double has sizeof==8) this adds the raw IEEE-754 bit patterns as integers, producing a meaningless value, and then reinterprets that integer back as the float/double result.
findings.triggeringInput: float buf[2] = {1.0f, 2.0f}; SuffixSums.Run<float>(buf, 2). Bits 0x3F800000 + 0x40000000 = 0x7F800000 are summed as ints, returning +Infinity instead of 3.0f. Likewise double over {1.0,2.0} gives garbage.
findings.rootCause: Dispatch is keyed only on sizeof(T)==4/8 and assumes the type is int/long. T:unmanaged also admits float, double, uint, ulong; for float/double the integer addition path is semantically wrong (and for uint/ulong it silently does signed arithmetic on values >Int32/Int64.Max).
findings.suggestedFix: Do not reinterpret arbitrary unmanaged T as integer for summation. Either constrain to numeric integer types via dedicated typed overloads (as already exist for int/long), or branch on typeof(T)==typeof(float)/typeof(double)/etc. and sum in the correct domain. Remove the sizeof-based int/long reinterpretation for the generic path.

findings.summary: RangeSum<T> uses the same sizeof(T)==4/8 -> int*/long* reinterpretation as Run<T>, so it sums float/double elements as integer bit patterns, yielding a wrong (or Infinity/NaN) result for floating-point types.
findings.triggeringInput: double buf[3] = {1.5, 2.5, 3.5}; SuffixSums.RangeSum<double>(buf, 0, 2) reinterprets each double's 64-bit pattern as a long, sums them, and reinterprets back, giving garbage instead of 7.5.
findings.rootCause: Type dispatch only inspects sizeof(T), not the actual element type, so float/double (and unsigned) elements are summed in the wrong numeric domain via pointer reinterpretation.
findings.suggestedFix: Branch on the concrete element type (typeof(T)) or provide explicit float/double/uint/ulong overloads, and accumulate in the correct domain instead of reinterpreting bytes as int/long.

findings.summary: Two-pointer pair counting undercounts when a and b contain duplicate values equal to half of (or complementary to) target. On a match it advances BOTH pointers once, counting only one diagonal pair instead of the full block of equal-valued duplicates, so the count of all (i,j) with a[i]+b[j]==target is wrong.
findings.triggeringInput: a=[1,1], aLen=2, b=[1,1], bLen=2, target=2. Returns 2 but the true number of pairs (i,j) with a[i]+b[j]==2 is 4.
findings.rootCause: When sum==target the code does left++ and right-- simultaneously, which only pairs index i with index j once and skips cross pairs among equal elements. The standard count-pairs-over-two-sorted-arrays algorithm must, on a tie, count the size of the equal-run in a multiplied by the equal-run in b (cntA*cntB), then skip both runs. Single-step advancement only works for the unique-element case.
findings.suggestedFix: On sum==target, count the number of consecutive equal elements at a[left] (cntA) and at b[right] (cntB), advance left by cntA and right by cntB, and add cntA*cntB to count (or, if a value equals its complement within the same run handling, treat accordingly). Alternatively document that arrays are required to be duplicate-free.

findings.summary: sum = a[left] + b[right] is computed as int+int and can overflow for representable int inputs, corrupting both the equality test and the pointer-advancement decision, yielding a wrong true/false.
findings.triggeringInput: a=[2000000000], aLen=1, b=[2000000000], bLen=1, target=-294967296. True sum 4000000000 overflows int to -294967296, so the method returns true even though no pair actually sums to -294967296; conversely large legitimate sums can be misrouted causing false negatives.
findings.rootCause: int arithmetic wraps on overflow; the comparison sum<target then steers the pointer in the wrong direction and the equality can spuriously match the wrapped value.
findings.suggestedFix: Compute the sum in long: long sum = (long)a[left] + b[right]; and compare against (long)target.

findings.summary: Same int+int overflow as HasPairWithSum: sum = a[left] + b[right] can wrap for representable ints, corrupting the comparison and miscounting.
findings.triggeringInput: a=[2000000000], aLen=1, b=[2000000000], bLen=1, target=-294967296. Wrapped sum equals target so count becomes 1 for a pair that does not actually sum to the target.
findings.rootCause: int overflow in a[left]+b[right] wraps, making sum==target spuriously true and sum<target steer the wrong pointer.
findings.suggestedFix: Use long sum = (long)a[left] + b[right]; and compare to (long)target.

findings.summary: In the bottom-up merge loop, the segment-boundary expression `l + 2 * width` (and `l + width`, `l += 2 * width`) overflows signed int once `width` reaches 2^30, corrupting the merge for very large `len`.
findings.triggeringInput: ptr to an array of len = 1073741825 (2^30 + 1) elements, e.g. T = byte (~1 GB allocation, valid under the unchecked contract). The width loop runs widths 1,2,...,2^30 (2^30 < len). At width = 2^30, l = 0: `l + 2*width` = 2147483648 overflows to int.MinValue (-2147483648).
findings.rootCause: `width` is an int that doubles up to the largest power of two below `len`. When `len > 2^30`, `width` becomes 2^30 and the arithmetic `Math.Min(l + 2 * width, len)` computes `0 + 2147483648`, which overflows int to -2147483648. Then `r = -2147483648`, `segLen = r - l` is negative (copy loop skipped, tmp left unfilled), `bEnd = r - l` negative while `aEnd = width = 2^30`, so the merge writes 2^30 uninitialized/garbage tmp entries back into ptr (wrong result, reading tmp beyond what was copied). Additionally `l += 2*width` overflows and the subsequent `width <<= 1` makes width = 2^31 (negative), so `while (width < len)` mis-iterates. This produces wrong output and out-of-range/uninitialized reads (UB).
findings.suggestedFix: Compute boundaries in 64-bit and clamp, e.g. `int m = (int)Math.Min((long)l + width, (long)len); int r = (int)Math.Min((long)l + 2L * width, (long)len);` and advance with `l = (int)Math.Min((long)l + 2L * width, (long)len);`, and guard the width doubling against overflow (use long for width or break when width >= len before shifting).

findings.summary: Hoare-partition quicksort excludes the returned boundary index p from both recursive halves. Partition returns j (the Hoare boundary), but the pivot in Hoare's scheme is NOT necessarily placed at its final sorted position at index j, so the correct recursion must include j in the left half ([lo, p] and [p+1, hi]). This code recurses on [lo, p-1] and [p+1, hi], dropping the element at index p from sorting. Result: array is left unsorted for many inputs.
findings.triggeringInput: int array {5,4,3,2,1,0}, Run(ptr,0,5). Produces 0 2 3 4 1 5 (not sorted). Also {3,1,2,3,3,3} -> 2 1 3 3 3 3.
findings.rootCause: Hoare partition (pivot = ptr[lo], returns j) guarantees ptr[lo..j] <= ptr[j+1..hi] but does NOT fix the pivot at index j. The standard correct recursion is Run(lo, j) / Run(j+1, hi). Here both branches treat p (=j) as a fixed pivot like Lomuto and exclude it: left branch uses Run(ptr, lo, p-1) then lo=p+1 (skips p), right branch uses Run(ptr, p+1, hi) then hi=p-1 (skips p).
findings.suggestedFix: For Hoare partition, include the boundary index in the left subarray. Change the introspective loop to: if (p - lo < hi - p) { Run(ptr, lo, p); lo = p + 1; } else { Run(ptr, p + 1, hi); hi = p; }. (Recurse on [lo, p] and [p+1, hi] instead of [lo, p-1] and [p+1, hi].)

findings.summary: Same Hoare-partition off-by-one as Run<T>. PartitionInt32 returns the Hoare boundary j, but RunInt32 recurses on [lo, p-1] and [p+1, hi], excluding index p from both halves even though the pivot is not guaranteed to be in final position at p. Array is left unsorted on many inputs.
findings.rootCause: PartitionInt32 is a Hoare partition (pivot = ptr[lo], returns j) which does not place the pivot at its final position at j. The correct recursion must include j on the left: RunInt32(lo, j) / RunInt32(j+1, hi). The code instead excludes p in both branches (Run(lo, p-1) with lo=p+1, and Run(p+1, hi) with hi=p-1).
findings.suggestedFix: Change the loop to: if (p - lo < hi - p) { RunInt32(ptr, lo, p); lo = p + 1; } else { RunInt32(ptr, p + 1, hi); hi = p; } so the boundary index p is included in the left subarray.

findings.summary: LSD radix sort on signed int does not flip the sign bit on the most-significant byte, so negative numbers (top byte 0x80-0xFF) sort AFTER non-negatives (top byte 0x00-0x7F), producing a wrong order whenever the array contains negative values.
findings.triggeringInput: int array {-1, 0} of len=2. Expected sorted {-1, 0}; produced {0, -1} because -1 has top byte 0xFF (placed after 0's top byte 0x00).
findings.rootCause: The final pass at shift=24 buckets by the raw most-significant byte and orders buckets 0..255 ascending. For two's-complement signed ints the sign bit is the high bit, so all negative values land in buckets 0x80..0xFF and are emitted after all non-negative values (buckets 0x00..0x7F). Counting-sort on the raw byte therefore treats negatives as larger than positives.
findings.suggestedFix: On the most-significant-byte pass, bias the byte by XOR 0x80 (i.e. use ((src[i] >> 24) & 0xFF) ^ 0x80) so the sign-bit ordering is corrected; equivalently offset all keys by adding 2^31 (as unsigned) before sorting.

findings.summary: Same signed-radix defect as Run: negatives sort after non-negatives. Additionally, the number of passes (4) is even, so after the final ping-pong swap the sorted data ends up in 'temp' (scratch), not in 'result', leaving wrong/garbage data in result.
findings.triggeringInput: int array ptr={-1,0}, len=2, result of size 2. (a) Sign bug: ordering is {0,-1} instead of {-1,0}. (b) Buffer bug: with len>1 and 4 passes (shifts 0,8,16,24), src/dst swap 4 times so the final write lands in temp; result holds the data from the 3rd pass, not the fully sorted output.
findings.rootCause: For an even number of radix passes the output buffer alternation ends with the last write into the local 'temp' buffer rather than the caller-provided 'result'. After the loop, src points at temp and result is never reconciled. Combined with the missing sign-bit handling, result is wrong both in order and in which buffer holds the answer.
findings.suggestedFix: Start the first pass writing into 'temp' and the second into 'result' (choose the initial dst so that after an even number of passes the final data lands in 'result'), or copy src back into result after the loop when src != result. Also apply the XOR-0x80 fix on the most-significant byte pass.

findings.summary: RunLong is fundamentally broken: it indexes the long* array as int* (only reads low 32 bits and only the first len/2 longs), shifts an int by up to 56 (no-op past 31 in C#), never advances/uses 'src', and never writes any result back to ptr. It does not sort longs at all.
findings.triggeringInput: long array {2, 1}, len=2. Expected {1,2}; ptr is left unchanged as {2,1} (and the high 32 bits / elements beyond index len/2 are never even examined).
findings.rootCause: Multiple defects: (1) ((int*)ptr)[i] reads 32-bit ints, so for i in [0,len) it touches only the first ceil(len/2) longs and never the high 32 bits of any long; (2) C# defines int<</>> shift counts mod 32, so for shift>=32 (the loop runs shift up to 56) '>> shift' equals '>> (shift&31)', making the high-byte passes read the same low bytes; (3) line 59 swaps into local t/tt but never assigns back to src/dst, and the loop body reads from ((int*)ptr) directly rather than src, so the ping-pong is meaningless; (4) the sorted data (if any) lives in temp/dst and is never copied back to ptr, so ptr is unmodified. Net effect: no sorting occurs.
findings.suggestedFix: Operate on long values, not int: compute the byte as (int)((src[i] >> shift) & 0xFF) where src is long* and shift ranges 0..56 over 64-bit longs; use proper long* src/dst ping-pong buffers; flip the sign bit (XOR 0x80) on the top byte (shift=56) for signed longs; and copy src back into ptr after the loop when src != ptr.

findings.summary: Build constructs the subsequence-automaton transition table with an off-by-one in the update order: it writes next[(i-1)*sigma+c] = last[c] BEFORE applying last[text[i-1]] = i. As a result, the transition for state (i-1) excludes the character at position i itself, so every state's 'next occurrence' table is shifted/missing one position. The whole automaton is corrupt, and the dependent Contains and CountDistinct return wrong results.
findings.triggeringInput: text = "ab" (bytes {0x61,0x62}), len=2, sigma=128. Produces next[0]['a']=0 (should be 1) and next[1]['b']=0 (should be 2). Then Contains(next, "a", 1, 128) returns false although 'a' is a subsequence of "ab"; Contains(next, "ab", 2, 128) returns false although "ab" is a subsequence; CountDistinct(next, 2, 128, 1000000007) returns 1 instead of the correct 3 (a, b, ab).
findings.rootCause: In the loop `for (int i = len; i >= 1; i--)`, the writes `next[(i-1)*sigma+c] = last[c]` for all c are done first, and only afterwards `last[text[i-1]] = i` is executed. State (i-1) must be able to reach the character that sits at position i (i.e. the next state should include position i), but because last is updated after the write, position i is never recorded into state (i-1)'s transitions. Concretely the first occurrence of any character is lost for the start state (state 0), and each state misses its immediately-following character. The standard build updates last (i.e. sets next[i][text[i]] = i+1) before/while copying the row.

findings.summary: Decode never emits output bytes and never sets *outLen; it only shifts input into a buffer and discards it. The method body has no traversal of the Huffman tree, no output[] writes, opos is never incremented, and *outLen is never assigned. Any call to decode produces zero correct output and leaves *outLen at its (possibly garbage) input value.
findings.triggeringInput: Any non-empty input, e.g. input pointing to 1 packed int produced by Huffman.Encode, inLen=1, *outLen preset to expected symbol count. Decode writes nothing to output and never updates *outLen.
findings.rootCause: The decode loop (lines 154-161) only fills `buffer` via `buffer = (buffer << 32) | (uint)input[ipos++]` and contains no symbol-decoding logic, no output writes, and no `*outLen = opos`. The algorithm is unimplemented.
findings.suggestedFix: Implement actual decoding: walk the Huffman tree (or use the codes) bit by bit from the buffer, write each decoded symbol to output[opos++], and on completion set *outLen = opos. Currently it returns no decoded data at all.

findings.summary: Out-of-bounds read of input when the best matching phrase extends to the end of the buffer. When a dictionary phrase of length pLen fully matches the remaining input but there is no following literal byte (i + pLen >= len), bestLen is still set to pLen+1, and line 46 reads input[i + bestLen - 1] = input[i + pLen], which is past the end of the valid input range.
findings.triggeringInput: input = {'a','a'} as bytes, len=2. First step emits phrase 0 with literal 'a' (i becomes 1). Second step: dictionary entry j=0 has pLen=1; inner loop runs k=0 (matches 'a'), k=1 has i+k=2 not < len so loop stops with match still true, so bestLen=pLen+1=2; then output[1].Literal = input[i + bestLen - 1] = input[1 + 1] = input[2], an out-of-bounds read; also i += 2 overshoots.
findings.rootCause: The match loop (lines 34-38) breaks on the `i + k < len` guard without distinguishing 'ran out of input' from 'matched a following literal'. A match that consumes the whole remaining input is still accepted as bestLen = pLen+1, but there is no real (pLen+1)-th literal byte, so input[i+pLen] is read out of range.
findings.suggestedFix: Only accept a phrase extension when the following literal actually exists: require `i + pLen < len` before setting bestLen = pLen+1 / bestPhrase = j+1. When the phrase matches to end-of-input with no trailing literal, do not extend (or emit the phrase without a literal via a distinct token).

findings.summary: Inverse BWT hardcodes the reconstruction start row to pos=0, but the correct start row is the matrix row whose suffix index is 0 (i.e. where sa[row]==0). Since Transform builds the BWT from a sentinel-less suffix array, whenever the original string is not the lexicographically smallest rotation (sa[0]!=0), Inverse returns a cyclic rotation of the original instead of the original, so the documented Transform/Inverse round-trip produces a WRONG result.
findings.triggeringInput: text=[3,1,2,1], len=4. Transform gives sa=[3,1,2,0], bwt=[2,3,1,1]. Inverse(bwt,4,...) returns text=[1,2,1,2] instead of [3,1,2,1].
findings.rootCause: The LF-mapping backward reconstruction (`int pos = 0; for i=len-1..0 { text[i]=bwt[pos]; pos=LF[pos]; }`) assumes row 0 of the sorted-rotation matrix corresponds to the original string's row. That holds only when sa[0]==0. The primary index (row where sa==0) produced by Transform is never stored, passed in, or recovered, so Inverse has no way to pick the right starting row. Additionally, because Transform uses a sentinel-less suffix-array BWT, strings with ambiguous/repeated rotations (e.g. [4,1,4,1,4]) are not uniquely invertible at all even with the correct start row.
findings.suggestedFix: Either (a) make Transform output a sentinel-terminated BWT and have Inverse start from the unique sentinel row, or (b) have Transform return the primary index p = the i with sa[i]==0 and pass it into Inverse to use as the starting pos instead of the hardcoded 0. With a proper sentinel the round-trip becomes well-defined for all inputs.

findings.summary: Query ignores pos and returns rules[ruleId].Char for BOTH terminal and non-terminal rules; non-terminal rules never have Char set (default 0) and the method never recurses into children, so any query into a non-terminal rule returns garbage instead of the character at position pos.
findings.triggeringInput: After Build on s="abab" (len=4) producing a non-terminal rule with id 0, call Query(rules, 0, 0). Both branches return rules[0].Char which was never assigned (==0), instead of 'a' (0x61).
findings.rootCause: Both branches of the if/else return rules[ruleId].Char. The non-terminal branch should decompose the rule by recursing into its child rules (Left/Right) using pos to pick the correct child and adjusted offset. The pos parameter is completely unused.
findings.suggestedFix: For a non-terminal rule, recurse: compute the expansion length of the left child; if pos < leftLen return Query(rules, leftChildId, pos) else Query(rules, rightChildId, pos-leftLen). This requires rules to store child rule IDs and expansion lengths, not raw string positions.

findings.summary: The 'find existing equal rule' deduplication can never succeed because rules store the absolute start position (Left=start) and compare rules[i].Left==start; start is strictly increasing across Build, so no prior rule ever has the same start. Every call creates a new rule, defeating the SLP's purpose of sharing repeated factors.
findings.triggeringInput: Build on s="aa"+"aa" style input where the same substring recurs at different positions: the two identical substrings are stored as distinct rules with different Left (start) values, so they are never merged into one shared rule.
findings.rootCause: Rules are keyed and matched by string position (start) rather than by content. Identical substrings at different positions have different start values, so rules[i].Left==start && rules[i].Right==len is never true for a previously seen substring, making FindOrCreate always Create.
findings.suggestedFix: Match rules by content: compare the actual byte sequence (or a hash) of s[start..start+len) against the bytes referenced by each existing rule, returning the existing id when the byte contents are equal. Storing positions only works if equal substrings always share identical positions, which they do not.

findings.summary: Build computes ruleId = FindOrCreateRule(...) but discards it; the top-level sequence of rules forming the program is never recorded anywhere, so the compressed string cannot be reconstructed. The produced 'rules' array also stores raw positions/lengths rather than child references, so it is not a usable straight-line program.
findings.triggeringInput: Build on any s with len>=2, e.g. s="abc" len=3: rules get populated but there is no output array/field listing which rule ids in which order reconstruct "abc"; the ruleId returned each iteration is dropped.
findings.rootCause: The return value of FindOrCreateRule is assigned to a local 'ruleId' that is never used, and Build has no out-parameter or structure capturing the top-level rule sequence. Combined with rules storing positions instead of child ids, the SLP is non-reconstructible.
findings.suggestedFix: Append each returned ruleId to a caller-provided output sequence (e.g. an int* program / out length), and define rules in terms of child rule ids so the program can be expanded back to the original string.

findings.summary: The new non-terminal symbol newSym=(byte)(254-ruleCount) can collide with byte values already present in the input or with symbols introduced by earlier rules, aliasing two different symbols to the same byte and corrupting the grammar (the rules array becomes ambiguous / non-decompressible).
findings.triggeringInput: input containing the byte 0xFE (254) with a repeated pair, len e.g. 4 = {0xFE,0xFE,0xFE,0xFE} as bytes. First rule uses newSym=254-0=0xFE, which is identical to the existing input symbol 0xFE, so the rule's pair (0xFE,0xFE) and the replacement symbol 0xFE are indistinguishable, making decompression ambiguous.
findings.rootCause: newSym is chosen from a fixed descending range (254,253,...) without verifying the value is absent from the current alphabet/work buffer. Input bytes are unrestricted (0..255), so the chosen non-terminal can equal an existing terminal or a previously created non-terminal.
findings.suggestedFix: Require/document that input alphabet is bounded (e.g. < some threshold) and assert newSym lies outside the used alphabet, or track used byte values and pick newSym from a guaranteed-free range; also guard ruleCount so 254-ruleCount cannot drop into the used range or below 0.

findings.summary: The flattened automaton format steals column 254 (output flag) and column 255 (fail link) out of the 256-wide transition row, but Query indexes the row directly with the raw text byte. When a text byte equals 254 or 255 the transition lookup reads the output-flag/fail-link slot instead of a real transition, producing wrong matches or jumping to a garbage state (potential out-of-range read). text is a plain byte* with no documented alphabet restriction, so bytes 0xFE/0xFF are valid inputs.
findings.triggeringInput: A state automaton built for pattern "a" (states[0*256+97]=1, states[1*256+254]=1 as output flag, states[1*256+255]=0 as fail link) queried over text={0x61,0xFE} (textLen=2): after consuming 'a' v=1; for byte 0xFE, line 17 reads states[1*256+254]=1 (the output flag) as a transition and sets v=1 again, and line 19 then reports a bogus match. With a larger output-flag value it would set v to an out-of-range state index.
findings.rootCause: Hardcoded magic indices states[v*256+254] (output) and states[v*256+255] (fail link) overlap the transition column space states[v*256+text[i]] for the same 256-wide row; bytes 254 and 255 collide with reserved metadata columns.
findings.suggestedFix: Reserve the metadata in extra columns (use a row width of 258 and put fail link at +256, output at +257), or document/enforce that the alphabet must be <=254 and reject/clamp text bytes >=254 (treat them as the no-transition / restart case).

findings.summary: Ukkonen 'edit distance <= k' is fundamentally broken: the core loop in PerformUkkonenIteration compares a[j] to b[j] at the SAME index (no diagonal offset) and never references lenA at all (only m = lenB is used). It does not compute Levenshtein distance. It returns wrong answers for almost all inputs: identical strings return false (distance reported > k even for k=0), and distant strings return true.
findings.triggeringInput: a={97,97} ("aa"), lenA=2, b={97,97} ("aa"), lenB=2, k=0 -> returns false, but true edit distance is 0 (<=0 should be true). Also a={97,98} ("ab"), b={98,97} ("ba"), k=1 -> returns true, but true edit distance is 2 (>1, should be false).
findings.rootCause: The diagonal extension uses 'a[j] != b[j]' with a single index j = i-1-v[i] for both strings, instead of advancing two distinct indices along a Myers/Ukkonen diagonal (e.g. a[x] vs b[x-diag]). lenA is never used, so the algorithm cannot account for differing string contents or lengths. The DP/greedy-extend recurrence does not correspond to edit distance.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace with a correct banded Levenshtein (the existing Levenshtein method already works) thresholded by k, or implement Myers' O(ND) diagonal algorithm properly: track furthest-reaching point on each diagonal h in [-d..d], compare a[x] vs b[x-h] while extending, and check x>=lenA && (x-h)>=lenB to declare distance d. As written it must use both lenA and lenB and a real diagonal offset.

findings.summary: Find records at most ONE run per period value. After recording (or even just matching) the first occurrence of a given period, the unconditional 'break' at the end of the matched-branch exits the entire 'start' loop, so all later non-overlapping runs of the same period are silently dropped. A method named after Main-Lorentz is expected to enumerate all maximal repetitions, but it misses many.
findings.triggeringInput: s={97,97,98,98} ("aabb"), n=4. Period 1 has two distinct runs: "aa" at start 0 (length 2) and "bb" at start 2 (length 2). Find returns count=1 with only {Start=0,Period=1,Length=2}; the "bb" run at Start=2 is never reported.
findings.rootCause: The 'break;' on line 54 is inside the 'for (start ...)' loop and runs after the first match for the current period, terminating the start scan. The subsumption-check loop was clearly intended to dedup overlapping runs of the same period across many starts, but the break prevents those later starts from ever being examined.
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the unconditional 'break;' (line 54) so the start loop continues scanning all positions for the current period; rely on the subsumption check (and/or advancing start past the found run) to avoid duplicate/overlapping reports. Optionally skip start forward to start+len-period after recording a run to avoid re-reporting the same maximal run from interior offsets.

findings.summary: Count iterates every index i and increments runs for each i lying inside an equal-LCP block, so a single run with a plateau of k equal LCP values is counted k times instead of once. The returned count is grossly inflated.
findings.triggeringInput: n=4, sa=[0,1,2,3] (any), lcp=[0,3,3,3]. Expected number of runs for this single plateau is 1, but Count returns 3 (it increments for i=1,2,3, each finding h>0 and block width>=2).
findings.rootCause: The loop has no de-duplication: for every i with lcp[i]>0 it re-expands the same maximal plateau and does runs++. Each of the (right-left+1) indices in one plateau triggers an independent increment, multiplying the count by the plateau width.
findings.suggestedFix: Count each maximal plateau once, e.g. only increment when i is the left boundary of its plateau (lcp[i-1] < h), or skip i past 'right' after counting a block. Concretely: after expanding, require i==left (i.e. lcp[left-1] < h) before runs++, or set i = right to advance past the counted block.

findings.summary: The per-node transition table is addressed at `(IntPtr)_node + cur*sizeof(Node) + sizeof(int)`, which points at the `Len` field (offset 4), not at the transition storage. Indexing `[c]` therefore aliases the node's own fields and adjacent nodes: c=0 overlaps `Len`, c=1 overlaps `Link`, c>=1 overlaps `Occ` / spill into the next node. SetNext(cur,c,state) overwrites Len/Link, corrupting the tree, and the -1 'no edge' sentinel is never actually stored in those slots (Init only sets `Next0` at offset 0, which transitions never read). Result: wrong distinct-palindrome counts and infinite loops on ordinary input.
findings.triggeringInput: Init(8) then Add(1) on an empty tree: returns 0 distinct palindromes, expected 1. A flat-memory simulation matching the exact pointer arithmetic gives wrong counts for inputs like [1] (got 0, exp 1), [0,0] (got 1, exp 2), and infinite loops for [0,1].
findings.rootCause: The base of the transition array adds an extra `sizeof(int)`, shifting the implicit transition slot from `Next0` (offset 0) to `Len` (offset 4). The transition slot for character c=0 thus IS the `Len` field, and higher c values overrun into `Link`, `Occ`, and neighboring nodes. Writing a transition value (a node index) into `Len`/`Link` corrupts the automaton, and reads of the transition return stale Len/Link/Occ values instead of -1, so existing-edge detection and the suffix-link walk both misbehave (wrong result or non-terminating while-loops). The node struct also reserves only a single int slot (`Next0`) for transitions, so any alphabet larger than 1 symbol writes out of the node and, near the end of the buffer, out of the `sizeof(Node)*(maxLen+3)` allocation.
findings.suggestedFix: Store transitions in a proper per-node array (e.g. give Node an `int Next[ALPHABET]` inline buffer or a separate `int* transitions` of size size*alphabet) and index it without the spurious `+ sizeof(int)` offset; initialize every transition slot to -1 in Init/when a node is created. At minimum, remove the `+ sizeof(int)` so the c=0 slot uses `Next0`, dedicate enough storage for the full alphabet, and set all slots to -1.

findings.summary: The eertree transition table does not exist: Node has only a single int field (Next0), but GetNext/SetNext treat each node as a 256-entry int[] indexed by the raw byte c (0..255), and additionally start the table at the wrong offset (+sizeof(int) lands on the Len field, not Next0). Both read and write therefore stride 4*c bytes past the node base, walking into neighbouring nodes' fields and far beyond the allocated buffer, corrupting Len/Link/Occ and causing heap out-of-bounds access (UB) for essentially every non-trivial input.
findings.triggeringInput: PalindromicTree.Build(s, 1) where s points to the single byte 97 ('a'). The buffer is sizeof(Node)*(1+3)=24*4=96 bytes (4 nodes). The first Extend(97) calls GetNext(1,97), which reads ((int*)((IntPtr)_node + 1*24 + 4))[97], i.e. byte offset 24+4+97*4 = 416 from _node base — ~320 bytes past the 96-byte allocation. Out-of-bounds heap read, followed by an out-of-bounds write in SetNext.
findings.rootCause: Node models the palindromic-tree (eertree) child transitions with a single int Next0, while the algorithm needs a per-node transition map over the alphabet. GetNext/SetNext compensate by indexing ((int*)ptr)[c] with c being a full byte (0..255), assuming 256 contiguous int slots per node that were never allocated. Worse, the base pointer is computed as node_base + sizeof(int), so index [0] aliases the Len field (offset 4) instead of Next0 (offset 0); for any positive byte value the access immediately leaves the node and, for typical character codes, leaves the allocated buffer entirely. Build only allocates sizeof(Node)*(len+3) bytes, with no room for any transition table.
findings.suggestedFix: Store transitions in a real per-node table. Either (a) add a fixed buffer to Node, e.g. 'public fixed int Next[256];' (or 26 for lowercase, mapping c-='a'), and have GetNext/SetNext index into that fixed buffer at the correct (offset-0) location: return _node[v].Next[c]; / _node[v].Next[c]=next; or (b) allocate a separate int[(len+3)*ALPHABET] transition array alongside the node array and index it as trans[v*ALPHABET + c]. Remove the erroneous '+ sizeof(int)' base adjustment, normalize/remap the byte to the chosen alphabet size, and size the allocation to include the table. Initialize all transition slots to -1.

findings.summary: The Earley parser has NO completer step and never advances a parent rule's dot past a nonterminal, and the final acceptance test does not require the completed rule to be the start rule. This makes it accept strings outside the language (false accepts).
findings.triggeringInput: rules = {rule0=[256,257,98], rule1=[257,97,-1]} (S -> T 'b', T -> 'a'); ruleCount=2; startRule=0; input="a" (len=1). L(S)={"ab"} so "a" must be rejected, but Parse returns true.
findings.rootCause: The main loop only implements the predictor (symbol>=256, lines 43-55) and scanner (lines 56-65). There is no completer: when a state with dot at end is found, line 41 just `continue`s, so no state with dot in the middle of a nonterminal is ever advanced. Separately, the final loop (lines 69-75) returns true for ANY completed state whose Origin==0 (line 73), never checking that S[...].Rule == startRule. The predicted child rule (rule1) completes over [0,1] with Origin 0, so the start rule's incomplete derivation is ignored and the string is wrongly accepted.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a completer: when a state (rule, dot=end, origin=o) completes in set k, scan set o for states whose next symbol is rules[rule*3] (the LHS) and add advanced copies (dot+1) into set k; loop until no new states (note this requires re-scanning set k as it grows). In the acceptance loop also require S[len*maxStates+i].Rule == startRule in addition to completeness and Origin==0.

findings.summary: Empty input (len==0) causes a zero-byte allocation followed by an out-of-bounds write, corrupting the heap / UB.
findings.triggeringInput: input=any, len=0, ruleCount=1, startRule=0. maxStates = 0*1*4 = 0, byteCount = 0, so S is a 0-byte allocation; line 27 writes S[0].Rule (12 bytes) out of bounds.
findings.rootCause: Line 18 computes maxStates = len * ruleCount * 4, which is 0 when len==0. Line 19 then allocates 0 bytes for S, but lines 27-30 unconditionally write the initial start state into S[0] and set counts[0]=1, writing past the zero-byte buffer.
findings.suggestedFix: Size maxStates with a floor, e.g. int maxStates = (len + 1) * ruleCount * 4 (or max(1, len) * ruleCount * 4), so at least one state set is allocated for the empty-input case; the final acceptance check at set len then works for len==0.

findings.summary: Empty input (len==0) leads to an out-of-bounds read dp[0][-1][startVar], which dereferences an unallocated/zero-length dp table (UB / crash).
findings.triggeringInput: input=any, len=0, prodCount=1, startVar=0. n=0, so the dp allocation loops never run (dp is a 0-byte pointer block), and line 48 reads dp[0][n-1] = dp[0][-1].
findings.rootCause: Line 12 sets n=len=0; line 13 allocates 0 bytes for dp and the population loops (lines 14-47) never execute. Line 48 unconditionally evaluates dp[0][n-1][startVar] = dp[0][-1][startVar], reading dp[0] (out of bounds of the 0-byte block) and then indexing [-1].
findings.suggestedFix: Special-case len==0 before allocating: return whether the empty string is accepted (typically false unless the grammar derives epsilon) instead of indexing dp[0][n-1].

findings.summary: Binary pattern search misses real occurrences when a suffix is a proper prefix of the pattern. Compare() only inspects min(patLen, textLen-sa[mid]) bytes; if those bytes all match (cmp==0) but the suffix is shorter than the pattern (patLen > textLen-sa[mid]), the suffix is lexicographically smaller than the pattern and the search must move right (l=mid+1). Instead the code only advances l when cmp<0, so it falls into the else branch (r=mid-1) and searches left, skipping the actual occurrence located to the right of mid. This returns -1 (not found) for patterns that are present.
findings.triggeringInput: text = {'a','a'} (textLen=2), sa = {1,0} (suffix order: "a" at idx1 < "aa" at idx0), pattern = {'a','a'} (patLen=2). Trace: l=0,r=1; mid=0,sa[0]=1; Compare(text+1,"aa",min(2,1)=1) -> 'a'=='a' => cmp=0; patLen(2)<=textLen-sa[0](1) is false so no return; cmp<0 false => else r=mid-1=-1; loop ends; returns -1. Correct answer is index 0 ("aa" occurs at 0).
findings.rootCause: When Compare returns 0 but the suffix is a proper prefix of the pattern (suffix shorter than pattern), the suffix is strictly less than the pattern lexicographically, yet the code treats cmp==0 (without the full-fit condition) as 'go left'. The 'suffix is a proper prefix of pattern => go right' case is not handled.
findings.suggestedFix: Treat a too-short suffix as less than the pattern. In the loop, after computing cmp, if cmp==0 and patLen > textLen - sa[mid], set l = mid + 1 (suffix < pattern). Concretely: if (cmp < 0 || (cmp == 0 && patLen > textLen - sa[mid])) l = mid + 1; else r = mid - 1; keeping the exact-match early return for cmp==0 && patLen <= textLen - sa[mid].

findings.summary: GetNext assumes each SuffixAutomaton.State contains an inline 256-int transition table, but State is {int Link; int Len; int Head} (12 bytes) and transitions live in a separate Edge[] linked list reachable via Head. It computes ptr = state + v*sizeof(State) + sizeof(int) and reads ((int*)ptr)[c] for c in 0..255, so c=0 reads Len, c=1 reads Head, and c>=2 reads other states / runs far past the array end. The whole class (Find, Dfs/CountSubstrings) is built on this and produces garbage plus out-of-bounds reads.
findings.triggeringInput: Any non-trivial automaton, e.g. SuffixAutomaton.Build over int text {0,1} producing >=3 states, then KthSubstring.Find(stPtr, stateCount, 1, ...). GetNext(0, 5, state) reads ((int*)(state + 0*12 + 4))[5] = bytes at offset 24..27, i.e. into state index 2's fields, instead of using the Head->Edge linked list. For c near 255 it reads ~1KB past state v, out of bounds for small automata.
findings.rootCause: Hand-rolled pointer arithmetic models a flat alphabet-indexed transition array that does not exist in this State layout; transitions are an Edge-array linked list keyed by Head, identical to SuffixAutomaton.GetNext(st,e,v,c).
findings.suggestedFix: Remove the custom GetNext and take the Edge* array as a parameter, walking the edge linked list (for (int edge=st[v].Head; edge!=-1; edge=e[edge].Next) if (e[edge].Char==c) return e[edge].To;) exactly like SuffixAutomaton.GetNext.

findings.summary: Even ignoring the GetNext layout bug, Find does not implement k-th distinct substring. It walks suffix links of the start node (v = state[v].Link) instead of descending through transitions, never decrements k while descending, never appends successive characters to build the answer, writes only outPtr[0]=c for the first matching char, and never sets *outLen. The k-th-distinct-substring algorithm must, at each state, scan outgoing transitions in char order, subtract per-edge counts from k, move into the chosen child, append its char, and repeat. Result is wrong length and wrong content.
findings.triggeringInput: Build SAM for text {0,1,1} ("abb"), call Find(stPtr, stateCount, 2, outLen, outPtr, dp): the function returns true after the first matching char from state 0 without descending, so outLen is left unset and the returned substring is not the 2nd distinct substring.
findings.rootCause: Wrong traversal (follows Link chain rather than transitions), no k accounting across descent, and no output of the full substring/outLen.
findings.suggestedFix: Descend from the initial state using transition counts: at each node iterate chars ascending, let cnt=CountSubstrings(child); if k<=cnt append char, k--, recurse into child; else k-=cnt. Set *outLen to the appended length. Also loop the alphabet over the real sigma (generalized SAM uses separators sigma+i >= 256), not a hardcoded 256.

findings.summary: Claims to return the k-th lexicographically-smallest substring but instead enumerates substrings ordered by (length, start index) and counts every occurrence with multiplicity (duplicates not removed). Both the ordering and the de-duplication are wrong for a lexicographic-k query.
findings.triggeringInput: text="ba" (bytes {'b','a'}), textLen=2, k=1. The loop yields len=1/start=0 -> "b" as count 1, so it returns "b". The 1st lexicographically-smallest distinct substring is "a" (sorted distinct: "a","b","ba"). Wrong result. For text="aa", k=2 it returns the second occurrence of "a" again rather than the next distinct substring "aa".
findings.rootCause: Enumeration is length-major / start-major, not lexicographic; and identical substrings at different start positions are counted multiple times.
findings.suggestedFix: Build a suffix automaton and descend transitions in ascending char order counting distinct substrings (CountSubstrings-style), or enumerate distinct substrings and sort lexicographically before indexing by k.

findings.summary: Stores outPos[count++] = lenPtr[v] (the state's Len) as if it were an occurrence position. Len is the substring length, identical for every state matching targetLen, not an end-position. The returned array is therefore just targetLen repeated and contains no real positions. Occurrence positions require endpos/firstpos data (propagated via the link tree from each cloned state's source), which this code never computes.
findings.triggeringInput: Build SAM for a text where two distinct states have Len==targetLen (e.g. "aab" with targetLen=1): the function returns count==(number of such states) but outPos is filled with [1,1,...], i.e. the length value, not the actual end positions of the substring.
findings.rootCause: Confuses state Len with position; SAM states do not store endpos here, and no firstpos propagation is done.
findings.suggestedFix: Track endpos: when building, record firstpos (end index) for each non-clone state and propagate the minimum/all positions up the suffix-link tree; emit those positions, not lenPtr[v].

findings.summary: Build does not implement Ukkonen's (or any correct) suffix-tree construction. The active point (activeNode/activeEdge/activeLen) is declared but never advanced — activeNode is hardwired to 0 (root) for the entire run, and matching only ever inspects the root's outgoing edge list by first character (edges[nextEdge].Char==c). The tree therefore can never branch below depth 1, no internal nodes / suffix links are created, and most suffixes are never inserted. The result is not a suffix tree for any string whose suffixes share a prefix.
findings.triggeringInput: s = {97,98,97} ("aba"), len=3. Trace: i=0 creates root edge Char=97 (suffix at 0); i=1 creates root edge Char=98 (suffix at 1); i=2 finds existing root edge with Char=97 so added=1 and i jumps to 3 WITHOUT inserting any node/edge for the suffix "a". The single-character suffix "a" (position 2) is silently dropped, and no internal node splitting "aba"/"a" is created. Querying the tree for the suffix "a" / position 2 fails. A correct suffix tree must represent all 3 suffixes "aba","ba","a".
findings.rootCause: The construction loop never walks down existing edges or updates the active point. It treats every position from the root and matches only the first character of root edges, so it builds a flat star of at-most-one-per-distinct-first-character edges instead of a proper trie/suffix tree. Edge.Min/Max are set to [i,len) (whole remaining suffix) on every new edge, and Edge.To/Node.Link/the activeEdge/activeLen machinery are never used to split or branch. Suffixes that share an initial character with an earlier-created edge are skipped entirely.
findings.suggestedFix: Replace the body with an actual Ukkonen implementation: maintain remainder count, advance (activeNode,activeEdge,activeLen) each step, walk-down along edges when activeLen exceeds the current edge length, split edges by creating an internal node when the next character mismatches, and set suffix links between the internal nodes created during the same phase. Alternatively, if only a suffix trie is intended, descend the current node's edge list character-by-character along the path (not just from the root) and create branching internal nodes on mismatch.

findings.summary: SuffixLowerBound returns the index AFTER a suffix that equals/prefix-matches the pattern instead of pointing at it. When the inner comparison loop ends with all compared characters equal (suffix has pattern as a prefix, or suffix == pattern), the local flag 'less' is never set to false, so the code falls into the 'else if (less) lo = mid + 1' branch and advances past the matching suffix. The first guard 'less && len < patLen && s[sa[mid]+len-1]==pattern[len-1]' also advances lo for a partial prefix match. Result: a true lower bound for a pattern that is present in the text returns one position too far, so the suffix array range used for occurrence counting/locating is wrong (e.g. reports a present pattern as having an empty or shifted range).
findings.triggeringInput: s = {1} (n=1), sa = {0}, pattern = {1}, patLen = 1. The only suffix "1" equals the pattern, so the lower bound must be 0, but the method returns 1. Another: s = {1,1,2,2,2,1}, sa = {5,0,1,4,3,2}, pattern = {1}, patLen = 1 returns 3 instead of 0.
findings.rootCause: The loop only distinguishes 'strictly less' (break with less=true) from 'strictly greater' (less=false), and never has a branch for the equal/prefix-match case. After the loop, less==true is treated unconditionally as 'suffix < pattern -> go right (lo=mid+1)'. There is no tiebreak like SuffixCompare's '(n - sa[mid]).CompareTo(patLen)' to keep hi=mid when the suffix matches the pattern prefix or is equal, so matching suffixes are skipped over.
findings.suggestedFix: Track three-way comparison like SuffixCompare. After comparing min(patLen, n-sa[mid]) chars, if all equal then the suffix starts with the pattern (a match) and should move hi = mid (not lo), so the lower bound points at the first matching suffix. Concretely: compute cmp by character; if cmp==0 after the loop, set less=false (treat prefix match / equal as NOT less) so the 'else hi = mid' branch runs. Remove the special 'len < patLen && s[...]==pattern[len-1]' clause, which incorrectly advances lo on a partial prefix match.
